projectTitle: Haverbrook Tickets: The Outage Every Dashboard Missed
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish DevOps build for a fictional event-ticket marketplace on AWS -- real infrastructure, CI/CD, and Kubernetes deployment taken from Terraform through EKS go-live, then a genuine monitoring blind spot where a real payment-processor outage caused a wave of silent checkout failures that every HTTP-status-based alert missed completely.
businessContext: Haverbrook Tickets is an online event-ticket marketplace with about 500,000 monthly active users. Two services, catalog-api and checkout-api, exist in a GitHub repo but only ever ran on developers' laptops -- no cloud infrastructure, no automated pipeline, and no real production monitoring. Celeste Marchbanks (VP of Engineering) and Marcus Oyelaran (the DevOps/Platform Engineer) build real AWS infrastructure, a CI/CD pipeline, and monitoring end to end -- but the error-rate alert they build defines 'error' as a non-2xx HTTP status code, and checkout-api's own existing payment-failure handling returns a 200 OK. When the external payment processor, VoltPay, has a real outage, every dashboard stays green while real customers silently can't check out, until Oscar Bennett's support team notices the complaints.
architectureSummary: AWS infrastructure provisioned with Terraform -- a VPC, an EKS cluster, ECR repositories for both services, and an RDS Postgres database. Both services containerized and built through a GitHub Actions pipeline (lint, test, build, vulnerability scan, push to ECR, deploy), rolled out to EKS across dev, staging, and prod namespaces with a manual approval gate before production. Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager provide monitoring, with a production error-rate alert defined on HTTP status codes. The real defect wasn't in the infrastructure, the pipeline, or the Kubernetes rollout -- it was in what the alert counted as an error, which never matched how checkout-api's own payment integration actually failed.

lessons.title: Meeting Haverbrook Tickets: Ships on a Laptop, Breaks in Production
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: Haverbrook Tickets' two services, catalog-api and checkout-api, exist only on developers' laptops with no cloud infrastructure, no automated pipeline, and no real production monitoring -- what you have to learn about the business before any AWS infrastructure gets built.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish DevOps build for a fictional online event-ticket marketplace, **Haverbrook Tickets** -- roughly 500,000 monthly active users buying tickets to concerts, sports, and theater. The company already has real code: a GitHub repository, `haverbrook/ticketing-platform`, holding two working services. The problem is everything *around* that code. Both services only run on developers' laptops today. There is no cloud infrastructure, no automated pipeline that tests and deploys a change safely, and no real production monitoring -- so deploys are manual, risky, and if something breaks after one ships, the team's first warning is usually a customer complaining to support, not a system telling them.

You are **Marcus Oyelaran**, the DevOps/Platform Engineer brought in to fix this end to end. This video starts exactly where every real build like this has to start: not with a Terraform file, not with a Kubernetes cluster, but with a meeting where you find out precisely what's broken today, who feels the pain, and how these two services actually work right now. By the end of this series, Haverbrook Tickets has real AWS infrastructure, a working CI/CD pipeline, and real monitoring -- but none of that gets designed until the problem is understood and written down, in the sponsor's own words, not yours.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school has two kids running a ticket table for the spring concert -- one kid writes down who wants which seat, and the other kid takes the money and hands out the tickets. Right now, both kids only do this work at their own kitchen tables at home, using their own laptops, and nobody else can see what they're doing. If one of them makes a change -- say, a new way of writing down seat numbers -- they just quietly start doing it differently the next day, and nobody finds out it caused a problem until a kid shows up to the concert with the wrong seat and complains.

That's Haverbrook Tickets today. Two important pieces of software -- one for browsing what's for sale, one for actually buying it -- only exist on two developers' personal laptops. There's no shared, safe place for the code to run where everyone can watch it, test it, and get warned the moment something goes wrong. Your job starts with sitting down with the person in charge, Celeste Marchbanks, and understanding exactly how risky that really is -- before you try to fix anything.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The detail that matters most in this discovery meeting isn't the headline -- 'we need to deploy to the cloud' -- it's the specific mechanics of what's missing and why that's dangerous at Haverbrook's actual scale. Haverbrook Tickets runs two services out of one GitHub repository, `haverbrook/ticketing-platform`: **catalog-api**, a Node.js service that serves event, venue, and ticket listings, with steady, read-heavy traffic; and **checkout-api**, a Python/FastAPI service that handles the cart and order submission, including a call out to an external payment processor, **VoltPay**, to actually charge the customer. checkout-api's traffic is nothing like catalog-api's -- it spikes hard the moment a popular show goes on sale, while catalog-api stays comparatively steady.

Neither service has ever run anywhere but a developer's laptop. There is no cloud infrastructure of any kind, no container registry, no orchestration layer, and no automated pipeline -- a code change goes from a developer's machine into production through manual steps, with no consistent testing, no vulnerability scanning, and no deployment history worth trusting. And once something does ship, there's no real production monitoring watching either service's actual health. **Celeste Marchbanks**, VP of Engineering, sponsors this project, and her stated worry is blunt: she wants deploys that are safe and automated, and she wants to actually know, in real time, when production is broken -- not find out from a customer. **Lin Chao**, the backend engineer who owns checkout-api's application code and its existing VoltPay integration, and **Ananya Reddy**, the site reliability engineer who will co-own monitoring and alerting with Marcus going forward, are the two people who can describe exactly how fragile the current manual process really is. **Oscar Bennett**, Customer Support Lead, is the person whose team is first to hear about problems from real customers today -- which is itself the clearest evidence that production visibility doesn't exist yet. Getting all of this precisely right now, in writing, is what keeps every later requirement in this series honest about what's actually broken versus what merely sounds risky.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk in already knowing what you don't know

Before the meeting, write down what you need to confirm, not just what you expect to hear:

- Do `catalog-api` and `checkout-api` run anywhere other than individual developers' laptops today?
- What actually happens, step by step, when someone wants to ship a change to either service right now?
- What, specifically, tells the team a deploy broke something in production today -- and is the honest answer "a customer complaint"?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and get the real problem in Celeste's own words

```
CELESTE:  Here's what keeps me up at night. Both of our services --
          catalog-api and checkout-api -- only run on laptops. We
          don't have a real cloud environment at all. When someone
          wants to ship a change, it's a manual process, and
          honestly, I'm not confident it's safe. And once something
          is live, we have no real way of knowing if it's actually
          working. I want deploys that are safe and automated, and I
          want to know when something breaks -- not find out from a
          customer three hours later.

MARCUS:   Walk me through what actually happens today when a
          developer wants to ship a change.

CELESTE:  Honestly? They test it on their own machine, they're
          careful, and then they manually push it somewhere that
          approximates production. There's no consistent process,
          no automated testing gate, nothing scanning for
          vulnerabilities, and no real deployment history we could
          point to and say "that's what's running right now."
```

## Step 3 -- Ask Lin Chao what shipping checkout-api actually looks like

```
MARCUS:  Lin, you own checkout-api's application code, including
         the VoltPay integration. Walk me through a real deploy.

LIN:     I test locally, I'm careful about the VoltPay calls
         especially since real money moves through them, and then I
         manually get the new code running wherever we're currently
         treating as "production" that day. There's no pipeline, no
         consistent test run, nothing scanning the container for
         known vulnerabilities before it goes out. If I make a
         mistake, the first sign is usually that something looks
         wrong in the logs, if anyone happens to be looking.

MARCUS:  And checkout-api's traffic -- is it steady, like
         catalog-api, or does it spike?

LIN:     It spikes hard. The moment a popular show goes on sale,
         checkout-api gets hit far harder than catalog-api ever
         does. catalog-api is just people browsing -- steady,
         read-heavy traffic all day. checkout-api is calm, then a
         wall of carts and orders all at once.
```

## Step 4 -- Ask Ananya Reddy what "knowing something broke" looks like today

```
MARCUS:   Ananya, if checkout-api started failing orders right now,
          how would we find out?

ANANYA:   Realistically? Oscar Bennett's support team starts getting
          tickets from customers whose cards got charged, or who
          think they bought a ticket and didn't. That's our alerting
          system today -- angry customers. We have no dashboards, no
          alerts, nothing watching either service's actual health in
          production. That's exactly the gap I want to close with
          Marcus.
```

## Step 5 -- Confirm the two services and their real shape

```
HAVERBROOK TICKETS -- CURRENT SERVICES

Service         Stack              Role                       Traffic
catalog-api      Node.js            Event/venue/ticket          Steady,
                                    listings                    read-heavy
checkout-api     Python/FastAPI     Cart + order submission,    Spiky --
                                    calls VoltPay to charge     ticket
                                    the customer                on-sales
                                                                cause real
                                                                spikes

Repository:   haverbrook/ticketing-platform (one GitHub repo, both
              services)
Today:        Both services run only on developers' laptops. No cloud
              infrastructure, no automated pipeline, no production
              monitoring.
```

## Step 6 -- Write the discovery summary and confirm it with Celeste

```
HAVERBROOK TICKETS -- DISCOVERY SUMMARY

Business problem:   Two production services, catalog-api and
                    checkout-api, run only on developers' laptops.
                    Deploys are manual and risky; there is no
                    automated testing, scanning, or deployment
                    pipeline, and no real production monitoring.
                    The team currently learns about production
                    problems from customer complaints, not from
                    any system.
Sponsor:            Celeste Marchbanks, VP of Engineering.
Key roles:          Lin Chao (Backend Engineer, owns checkout-api's
                    app code and its VoltPay integration), Ananya
                    Reddy (SRE, will co-own monitoring/alerting),
                    Oscar Bennett (Customer Support Lead, first to
                    hear about problems from real customers today).
Repository:         haverbrook/ticketing-platform.
```

Send this summary to Celeste Marchbanks and ask directly: "Did I capture this accurately?" Every requirement written in the next lesson traces back to a line in this document -- and her sign-off on the real pain is what keeps that requirement honest about what actually needs to change.

Repo confirmed as haverbrook/ticketing-platform.

lessons.title: Turning 'Ship Safely and Know When It Breaks' Into a Testable Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Celeste Marchbanks's 'ship safely and know when it breaks' into one precise, testable requirement: a code push to GitHub results in an automated, tested, scanned deployment to a real environment, and the team gets paged when the business outcome -- a customer actually completing a purchase -- is failing, not merely when an HTTP status code looks bad.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Discovery gave you a real problem and an honest picture of Haverbrook Tickets' current footprint -- but 'ship safely and know when it breaks' isn't a requirement yet, it's an intention. This lesson turns that intention into one precise, written requirement you can actually design against and, eventually, test.

The requirement has two parts. First, a code push to the `haverbrook/ticketing-platform` repository on GitHub must result in an automated pipeline -- the change gets linted and tested, the resulting container gets scanned for known vulnerabilities, and only then does it deploy to a real environment. No more manual, one-off deploys from a laptop. Second, and just as important, the team must get paged when something is *actually* broken in production -- and 'actually broken' is defined deliberately narrowly: not when an HTTP status code merely looks bad, but when the real business outcome, a customer successfully completing a ticket purchase, is failing. Those are genuinely different signals, and collapsing them into one is exactly the kind of mistake this requirement is written to prevent. Whether the monitoring this series eventually builds fully lives up to that second half is something to verify honestly later -- not something to assume solved just because it's written down now.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the two kids running the ticket table finally agree their system needs fixing. 'Make it safer' doesn't tell anyone what to build. So they get specific: from now on, before any new way of writing down tickets goes live, somebody has to check it actually works and isn't full of holes, on a real table set up just for testing -- not just 'I was careful.' And just as important: if a kid tries to buy a ticket and it doesn't actually work, somebody has to find out right away -- not because the table *looked* fine from across the room, but because they actually checked whether the kid walked away with a real ticket in hand.

That's the requirement for Haverbrook Tickets. Every change gets automatically checked and tested before it goes live, on a real setup, not a laptop. And the team gets alerted the moment a customer can't actually finish buying a ticket -- not just when some technical light turns red that might not mean anything real.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and 'ship safely and know when it breaks' is exactly that until it's pinned to a precise pipeline standard and a precise definition of 'broken.'

The pipeline half is the more straightforward of the two: every push to haverbrook/ticketing-platform triggers lint and test, a container vulnerability scan, and then deployment to a real environment -- no manual, ad hoc deploys from anyone's laptop, ever again. That's concrete enough to build and concrete enough to verify later.

The alerting half deserves the most care, because it's the one most likely to get quietly simplified into something weaker than what's actually needed. It would be easy to build alerting around HTTP status codes -- page someone when checkout-api starts returning 500s -- and call that 'knowing when it breaks.' That's not what Celeste Marchbanks is actually asking for. Her real worry, stated plainly in the first meeting, is whether the team will actually know when something is broken in production -- and a service can be returning a perfectly healthy-looking HTTP 200 while the underlying business outcome, a customer successfully completing a purchase and having VoltPay actually charge them, is quietly failing. This requirement commits, in writing, to paging on that real business outcome -- not merely on status codes -- as the standard this project is building toward. It does not yet claim that the monitoring stack, Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager, actually catches every real way checkout-api could fail while still returning healthy-looking responses. That's genuine configuration and design work still ahead, and whether it actually holds up is something this series needs to test honestly once it exists, not assume is solved because the requirement sounds right on paper.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the real constraint out of Celeste's side of the business

```
MARCUS:    You said 'ship safely and know when it breaks' in the
           first meeting. What would actually have to be true for
           you to call that delivered?

CELESTE:   Two things. First, nobody should ever manually push code
           to production again -- every change gets tested and
           scanned automatically before it goes anywhere real.
           Second, I need to actually know when production is
           broken. And I mean really broken -- a customer trying to
           buy a ticket and failing -- not some technical signal
           that might not mean anything to an actual customer.

MARCUS:    Can you say more about that second part? What's the
           difference, in your mind?

CELESTE:   checkout-api could come back with a perfectly fine-looking
           response and still have failed to actually charge the
           customer or finish the order. I don't want us paged
           because a status code looked bad. I want us paged because
           a real purchase didn't go through.
```

## Step 2 -- Fix the exact requirement in writing

```
REQUIREMENT -- HAVERBROOK TICKETS SHIP SAFELY (V1)

REQ-1: Every push to haverbrook/ticketing-platform triggers an
       automated pipeline -- lint and test, a container vulnerability
       scan, and deployment to a real environment. No manual,
       one-off deploys from a developer's laptop.
REQ-2: The team gets paged when the real business outcome -- a
       customer successfully completing a ticket purchase -- is
       actually failing in production. An HTTP status code looking
       healthy or unhealthy is not, by itself, sufficient evidence
       either way.
```

## Step 3 -- Say out loud what REQ-2 doesn't promise yet

```
MARCUS:    I want to be clear about one thing. REQ-2 is the
           requirement -- we page on real purchase failures, not
           status codes. It's not yet a claim that our monitoring
           actually catches every way checkout-api could fail while
           still looking healthy from the outside. That's real
           design work ahead of us, with Ananya, and I want to test
           it honestly once it exists.

CELESTE:   That's fair -- I just need to know that's the standard
           we're actually building toward, and that someone checks
           it once it's live.
```

## Step 4 -- Sanity-check the requirement against a real scenario

```
Scenario: During a popular on-sale, checkout-api calls VoltPay to
          charge a customer. VoltPay has an internal issue and the
          charge never actually completes -- but checkout-api's own
          endpoint still returns an HTTP 200, because the request
          itself was handled without an application error. Under
          REQ-2, this has to be detectable and page the team, because
          the customer did not actually get a ticket -- even though
          every status code involved looked fine.
```

Walk this scenario past Celeste and Ananya Reddy directly and ask: "Is this exactly what you mean by knowing when it breaks?"

## Step 5 -- Get the requirement signed off

Save REQ-1 and REQ-2 alongside the Lesson 1 discovery summary. Get explicit sign-off from Celeste Marchbanks on REQ-2 specifically -- the business-outcome standard is the line most likely to get quietly reinterpreted later as "the status codes look fine, so it must be fine," once real traffic starts flowing through a live pipeline.

Flagged explicitly to Celeste that REQ-2's accuracy depends on monitoring design work still ahead, not something already solved.

Celeste has signed off in writing, which is what every later design decision in this project gets measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'ship safely and know when it breaks' into a specific, measurable commitment: every code change is automatically tested and scanned before it goes live, and we get alerted based on whether customers can actually complete a purchase -- not just whether a technical status code looks fine.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: Two Services, One Pipeline, Real Monitoring
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what V1 actually ships -- AWS infrastructure, a CI/CD pipeline, and real monitoring for catalog-api and checkout-api -- and naming what's explicitly deferred: rebuilding either service's own application code, a multi-region/disaster-recovery setup, and anything touching VoltPay or payment processing logic itself.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have a precise, signed-off requirement. Before any Terraform file gets written or any cluster gets provisioned, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this build actually delivers -- and, just as importantly, what it explicitly does not. For Haverbrook Tickets, V1 ships three things: real AWS infrastructure for catalog-api and checkout-api; a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline that lints, tests, scans, and deploys both services automatically; and real monitoring and alerting -- Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager routing to Slack/PagerDuty -- built around the business-outcome standard from the previous lesson.

What's explicitly out of scope, named in writing rather than left to assumption, is anything beyond that infrastructure-and-pipeline core. This project does not rewrite or redesign catalog-api's or checkout-api's own application code -- Lin Chao and the rest of the application team keep owning that, including checkout-api's existing VoltPay integration, exactly as it works today. It does not add a multi-region or disaster-recovery setup -- a real, valuable idea, deliberately deferred and named rather than quietly dropped. And it does not replace VoltPay or touch payment processing logic itself in any way -- VoltPay stays exactly as Lin Chao's team has already integrated it; this project's job is to safely deploy and monitor the services that call it, not to change how they call it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the two kids running the ticket table finally get real help: a grown-up agrees to build them a proper, safe table setup, with a checklist for every new idea before it's used for real, and a way to know right away if something stops working. A good helper like that does one job well: it gives the ticket table a safe place to run, checks every change automatically, and watches for real trouble. A helper who also tried to rewrite how the kids decide who gets the good seats, or build a brand-new backup ticket table in a whole different town just in case the first one burns down, or change how the kids' parents' credit cards actually get charged, would be doing a much bigger job than anyone asked for -- and the actual safe table might never get finished.

This project is that real helper, doing exactly the first job well. It doesn't rewrite the kids' own rules for selling tickets, it doesn't build a whole second town's worth of backup tables yet, and it doesn't touch how the money itself gets charged.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here specifically because a working CI/CD pipeline and real infrastructure are unusually tempting things to over-extend once they exist. The moment catalog-api and checkout-api are running safely in the cloud with real monitoring, it's natural for stakeholders to ask 'can we also use this project to clean up checkout-api's own business logic?' or 'should we also build a second region in case this one goes down?' or 'can we swap VoltPay while we're in here?' All three are reasonable questions, and none of them belong in V1.

Application code is deferred because it has a different, already-established owner: Lin Chao and the backend team own catalog-api's and checkout-api's business logic, including checkout-api's existing VoltPay integration, and this project's job is to build the infrastructure and pipeline that deploys and monitors that code safely -- not to rewrite it. Multi-region and disaster recovery are deferred because they're real future work with a name of their own: call it a future **Haverbrook Tickets Multi-Region Resilience** initiative, V2, so it doesn't get lost as a vague someday -- V1 proves out a single-region AWS footprint first, which has to work before a second region is worth building. And VoltPay itself, and the payment processing logic that calls it, is deferred for the clearest reason of all: it is Lin Chao's application code and a live third-party payment integration, and swapping or redesigning it is a different, much higher-risk project with different owners and different compliance considerations -- this project's only interest in VoltPay is making sure the service that calls it is deployed safely and that the team actually finds out if that call quietly stops working. What V1 commits to is narrower and fully ownable: AWS infrastructure for both named services, one CI/CD pipeline, and real monitoring built around the business-outcome standard from the previous lesson -- not an application rewrite, not a second region, and not a payments project.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: AWS, EKS, ECR, and Terraform
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: AWS as the cloud provider, Amazon EKS for orchestration, Amazon ECR as the container registry, Terraform for infrastructure as code, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and Prometheus/Grafana for monitoring -- each justified against a real alternative, grounded in checkout-api's spiky ticket-on-sale traffic and catalog-api's steady read-heavy load.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly which technologies Haverbrook Tickets' infrastructure is built on. The stack this lesson fixes is **AWS** as the cloud provider; **Amazon EKS** (Kubernetes) for orchestration, with `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` namespaces; **Amazon ECR** as the container registry; **Terraform** provisioning the VPC, the EKS cluster, the ECR repositories, and an RDS Postgres database; **GitHub Actions** running lint/test, build, a container vulnerability scan, push to ECR, and deploy; and **Prometheus and Grafana** for monitoring, with **Alertmanager** routing alerts to Slack and PagerDuty.

Each choice earns its place against a real alternative, not just convention. The decision this lesson spends the most time on is Kubernetes itself: why EKS instead of a simpler platform-as-a-service like AWS Elastic Beanstalk, ECS Fargate, or a managed PaaS such as Heroku or Render. That decision traces directly back to checkout-api's real traffic shape -- steady for catalog-api, but spiking hard the moment a popular show goes on sale -- and to REQ-2's demand for real, business-outcome-aware alerting, which needs infrastructure the team can actually instrument and control, not a black box. This lesson fixes the stack. It does not yet claim the stack alone guarantees REQ-1 and REQ-2 are met -- that depends on how the pipeline and monitoring are actually configured against it, which is real work still ahead in this series, not something to assume solved just because the right technologies were chosen.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the grown-up helping the ticket table finally has to decide what kind of table to actually build. They could buy a simple folding table that's easy to set up but can only ever be one size -- fine for a quiet afternoon, but it would collapse the second a hundred kids rushed the table all at once for a popular show. Or they could build a table that's designed from the start to grow extra legs and extra space the instant a crowd shows up, and shrink back down once the rush is over. For Haverbrook, where ticket on-sales really do cause a sudden rush, the grow-and-shrink table is worth the extra setup work, because the simple folding table would fall over exactly when it matters most.

The helper also picks a specific toolbox for building and checking the table (Terraform and GitHub Actions), a specific shelf to store the finished table parts on before they're used (Amazon ECR), and a specific set of gauges to watch the table's health (Prometheus and Grafana). None of these are the only tools that could work -- they're the ones that fit Haverbrook's actual situation best.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every technology on this list traces back to a real requirement from the first three lessons, not a default stack someone copied from a conference talk.

Start with AWS as the cloud provider: Haverbrook Tickets has no existing cloud footprint to build around, so this decision is about picking the ecosystem with the deepest managed-Kubernetes, container-registry, and relational-database tooling to build the rest of the stack on top of -- EKS, ECR, and RDS Postgres all being first-party, tightly integrated AWS services is what makes the rest of this list coherent rather than a pile of unrelated tools.

The decision that deserves the most scrutiny is EKS over a simpler option like ECS Fargate or a PaaS such as Heroku or Render. A PaaS would genuinely be simpler to operate for catalog-api alone, which has steady, read-heavy, fairly predictable traffic. checkout-api is the service that rules that out: its traffic spikes hard and fast the moment a popular show goes on sale, and Haverbrook needs real, fine-grained control over autoscaling behavior -- how fast new pods come up, how resource requests and limits are tuned per service, how traffic is load-balanced across them -- that a simpler PaaS deliberately abstracts away specifically so operators don't have to think about it. Kubernetes, and EKS as AWS's managed flavor of it, hands that control back, at the cost of real operational complexity this series has to take seriously rather than wave away. Running both services as Kubernetes workloads in the same cluster, split across dev/staging/prod namespaces, also means catalog-api's steady load and checkout-api's spiky load can be reasoned about and scaled independently within one coherent platform, instead of forcing both services onto identical infrastructure assumptions that only really fit one of them.

ECR is the natural container registry choice once EKS is chosen -- it's the first-party AWS registry with the tightest IAM and networking integration into the cluster, over running a self-hosted registry or paying for a separate third-party one with no clear advantage here. Terraform is chosen over manually clicking through the AWS console, or a cloud-specific tool like CloudFormation, because it is a declarative, version-controlled definition of the VPC, the EKS cluster, the ECR repositories, and the RDS Postgres database -- reviewable in a pull request before anything real changes, which matters enormously for a team that has never had any infrastructure at all until now. GitHub Actions is chosen because the code already lives on GitHub, in haverbrook/ticketing-platform, making it the pipeline with the least new surface area to adopt, over a separate CI system like Jenkins or CircleCI that would mean standing up and maintaining a whole additional system. And Prometheus and Grafana, with Alertmanager routing to Slack and PagerDuty, are chosen over a pure-SaaS observability platform because they run natively inside the same EKS cluster and scrape metrics directly from workloads running there, giving the team direct control over exactly what gets measured and alerted on -- which matters because REQ-2 demands alerting tied to a real business outcome, not just infrastructure-level signals, and that kind of custom instrumentation is squarely the kind of work this stack is built to support. None of this is itself proof that REQ-1 and REQ-2 are actually satisfied -- that depends on how the pipeline stages and the alerting rules are actually built against this stack, which is real work for the implementation lessons ahead.
