lessons.title: Planning the CI/CD Pipeline: Build, Scan, Deploy
lessons.summary: Planning the GitHub Actions pipeline that will carry catalog-api and checkout-api from pull request to deployable container -- lint/test, build, a Trivy vulnerability scan gate, push to Amazon ECR tagged with the git SHA, then deploy -- before a single workflow file gets written.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With catalog-api and checkout-api finally about to leave developer laptops, Marcus Oyelaran's first real planning job is deciding exactly how code gets from a pull request into a running container, safely and the same way every time. This lesson plans the GitHub Actions pipeline that both services will share: lint and automated tests on every pull request, a container image build, an automated vulnerability scan of that image, a push to Amazon ECR tagged with the commit's git SHA, and only then a deploy.

Nothing gets built in this lesson -- no workflow YAML lives in the repo yet, no pipeline has run. This is the plan Marcus works out, and the reasoning behind each stage, before he or anyone writes a single `.github/workflows` file. That writing happens in a later implementation lesson, once the plan below has been checked against how Lin Chao's team actually ships checkout-api changes today.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a package that has to travel from a workshop to a customer's door. Before it's allowed on the truck, a few checkpoints have to happen in order: someone checks the item was built correctly, someone inspects it for anything dangerous packed inside, the box gets a permanent tracking label that can never be reused for a different package, and only then does it go on the truck.

That's the plan Marcus is drawing up for Haverbrook Tickets' code. Every change to catalog-api or checkout-api has to pass its tests, get built into a container, get checked for known security problems, and get a permanent label -- the exact commit it came from -- before it's allowed anywhere near a real customer. If the security check finds something seriously wrong, the package doesn't get labeled or loaded onto the truck at all. This lesson is Marcus deciding what order those checkpoints happen in and why, not building the conveyor belt yet.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The pipeline plan has four stages, and the order is deliberate rather than arbitrary. Lint and automated tests run first, against every pull request, because they're the cheapest possible check to fail on -- there's no reason to spend build minutes producing a container image for code that doesn't even pass its own test suite. Only a pull request that passes lint/test triggers a container build.

The build stage produces one image per service, tagged with the pull request's or merge commit's git SHA rather than a mutable tag like `latest`. This matters operationally: a SHA-tagged image is traceable back to the exact source that produced it, which means a rollback is "redeploy the previous SHA" rather than "hope the registry still has the right thing under a tag someone may have already overwritten."

The vulnerability scan runs against the built image, using a scanner such as Trivy, before the image is pushed to Amazon ECR. This is planned as a hard gate, not an advisory step: a critical-severity finding blocks the pipeline from pushing the image or proceeding to deploy, the same way a failing test does. The reasoning Marcus brings to Celeste Marchbanks and Lin Chao is specific to what these two services actually are -- checkout-api sits directly in front of VoltPay and handles real payment data in transit, which makes a known-exploitable base image or dependency a materially different kind of risk than it would be for, say, an internal reporting tool. Blocking the merge or the deploy on a critical finding costs engineering time in the moment; shipping a known critical vulnerability into the path that touches payment processing costs more later, and that tradeoff is the plan's actual justification, not a boilerplate security requirement.

Only an image that has passed lint/test and the scan gate gets pushed to Amazon ECR, into a repository scoped per service, still tagged by git SHA. The deploy stage that follows -- which environment it targets, and under what rollout strategy -- is intentionally left to the Kubernetes planning lesson that follows this one; this lesson's job is only the build-scan-push sequence and the gate logic that governs it.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the two things the pipeline has to protect

Marcus starts from what's actually true about catalog-api and checkout-api today: both exist only as code on developer laptops, both will move through the same shared pipeline shape, and checkout-api is the one that calls VoltPay and handles real payment submissions. The plan treats that last fact as the reason the pipeline needs a real security gate, not a cosmetic one -- a vulnerability in checkout-api's image is a materially different risk than the same vulnerability in catalog-api's.

## Step 2 -- Plan the trigger and the lint/test stage

Every pull request against either service's repository triggers the pipeline. The first stage runs linting and the service's existing automated test suite -- Node.js tooling for catalog-api, pytest for checkout-api's FastAPI codebase. This stage is planned to run before any container gets built, because it's the cheapest failure to catch early:

```yaml
# planned shape, not yet written to .github/workflows/
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  lint-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: <service-specific lint + test command>
```

A pull request that fails lint/test never reaches the build stage at all.

## Step 3 -- Plan the build stage and the tagging convention

Once lint/test passes, the plan calls for a Docker build producing one image per service, tagged with the triggering commit's git SHA -- never `latest`. The plan names this explicitly because a mutable tag makes rollback ambiguous; a SHA tag makes "redeploy exactly what was running two releases ago" a real, checkable operation rather than a guess.

## Step 4 -- Plan the vulnerability scan as a hard gate

Immediately after build, the plan inserts a vulnerability scan of the built image using a scanner such as Trivy, before the image goes anywhere near Amazon ECR. The plan fixes the gate's behavior: a critical-severity finding fails the pipeline and blocks both the push to ECR and any deploy, the same way a failing unit test does. Lower-severity findings are planned to surface as pipeline output for the team to triage, without blocking merge on their own -- a decision Marcus checks with Celeste and Lin Chao rather than assuming unilaterally, since an overly strict gate on medium/low findings risks the team routing around it instead of fixing root causes.

```yaml
  build-scan:
    needs: lint-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: docker build -t <service>:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 <service>:${{ github.sha }}
```

## Step 5 -- Plan the push to Amazon ECR

Only an image that cleared both the test suite and the scan gate gets pushed. The plan calls for one Amazon ECR repository per service -- a `catalog-api` repository and a `checkout-api` repository -- with every pushed image tagged by git SHA, matching the build stage's tagging convention.

## Step 6 -- Leave deploy to the next planning lesson, on purpose

The plan stops at "image pushed to ECR, tagged by SHA." Which EKS namespace a given image actually gets deployed into, and under what rollout strategy, is deliberately scoped to the Kubernetes planning lesson that follows -- this lesson's job is the build-scan-push sequence and the gate logic, not the deploy step itself. Marcus brings this four-stage plan, and the specific reasoning for gating hard on critical vulnerabilities, to Celeste Marchbanks for sign-off and to Lin Chao to confirm it doesn't conflict with how her team already ships checkout-api changes.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned a four-stage GitHub Actions pipeline shared by catalog-api and checkout-api: lint/test on PR, a Docker build tagged by git SHA (never latest), a Trivy scan gated to hard-fail on critical findings before push, then push to per-service Amazon ECR repositories. Deploy mechanics are explicitly deferred to the Kubernetes planning lesson. Nothing is implemented yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned the exact sequence code will travel through before it reaches customers: automated tests, a container build, a security scan, and a push to our image registry, with the security scan able to block a release if it finds something critical. This is the plan only -- we'll build the actual pipeline in an upcoming implementation step.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned the quality and security checkpoints every code change to the ticketing and checkout systems will have to pass before it can go live, including a hard stop if a serious security issue is found in the build -- especially important given checkout-api handles real payment submissions through VoltPay.

lessons.title: Planning Kubernetes Namespaces, Resources, and Rollout Strategy
lessons.summary: Planning the EKS environment shape -- dev/staging/prod namespaces, resource requests and limits sized differently for read-heavy catalog-api versus spiky checkout-api, and a rolling-update rollout strategy with readiness probes and staged promotion through environments.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the CI/CD pipeline's shape planned in the last lesson, Marcus Oyelaran now plans where the images that pipeline produces will actually run. This lesson plans the Amazon EKS environment structure: separate `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` namespaces, resource requests and limits sized around how catalog-api and checkout-api actually behave under load, and a rollout strategy -- rolling updates with readiness probes, promoted stage by stage through the three environments.

This is still planning, not manifests. No Deployment YAML gets written in this lesson; the actual Kubernetes manifests are built in a later implementation lesson, once this plan has been checked against what Ananya Reddy's monitoring setup will need to observe and what Lin Chao's team needs from a deploy in order to trust it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine two different food stalls at a busy fair. One sells a steady trickle of printed programs all day long -- predictable, easy to staff. The other sells tickets right before the headline act starts, where nothing happens for an hour and then two hundred people show up in five minutes. You wouldn't staff both stalls the same way, and you wouldn't put them in the same tent with no walls between them either, because a line out the door at the ticket stall shouldn't knock over the program table.

That's what Marcus is planning here: separate "tents" (namespaces) for testing, a dress rehearsal, and the real show (dev, staging, prod), and different staffing plans (resources) for the steady program stall (catalog-api) versus the bursty ticket stall (checkout-api). He's also planning how a new batch of staff ever gets swapped in without the stall ever actually closing -- a few at a time, checking each new staffer is ready before sending the old one home.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Three namespaces per EKS cluster -- `dev`, `staging`, `prod` -- give Marcus a consistent promotion path and a clean boundary for RBAC and resource quotas later, without standing up three separate clusters. The plan commits to namespace-level isolation as sufficient at Haverbrook Tickets' current scale, revisiting dedicated clusters only if a future compliance or blast-radius requirement demands it.

Resource requests and limits are planned around the two services' actual traffic shape rather than a single default copied across both. catalog-api is read-heavy listings traffic: comparatively steady, cacheable, and predictable enough to plan tight, well-understood requests/limits and a modest, mostly-static replica count. checkout-api is the cart-and-order-submission path behind VoltPay, and its traffic is explicitly spikier -- ticket on-sales and popular events can drive a burst far above its baseline. The plan calls for checkout-api to run with more generous limits relative to its request, headroom for horizontal autoscaling to react to a real spike, and closer attention to what "spiky" does to connection pools and in-flight request counts under load. The plan does not yet fix exact CPU/memory numbers in this lesson -- those get set once real load data exists from staging -- but it commits to sizing the two services differently rather than applying one template to both, and to checkout-api getting the autoscaling headroom catalog-api does not need as urgently.

The rollout strategy is planned as a rolling update, each new version brought up pod by pod behind a readiness probe, with the old version only torn down once the new one reports ready -- avoiding a hard cutover that could drop in-flight requests, which matters more for checkout-api given it's mid-transaction traffic rather than catalog-api's read-only listings. Promotion is planned as staged: an image that passed CI lands in `dev` first, gets validated, promotes to `staging` for a closer-to-production check, and only then promotes to `prod`. The plan deliberately leaves the specific promotion gates (automated checks vs. manual approval at each stage) for the implementation lesson, and leaves exactly what "healthy" means for the readiness probe -- a question that matters more once checkout-api's own behavior under payment-processor slowness gets understood -- open for now.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Plan the namespace structure

The plan calls for three namespaces inside the single EKS cluster Terraform will provision: `dev`, `staging`, and `prod`. Each namespace holds both services -- catalog-api and checkout-api -- so promotion through environments always moves both services' manifests together rather than letting one drift ahead of the other. Namespace-level isolation is judged sufficient for Haverbrook Tickets' current scale; a dedicated cluster per environment is explicitly not planned unless a future requirement forces it.

```text
# planned shape, not yet applied
eks cluster: haverbrook-tickets
  namespace: dev
  namespace: staging
  namespace: prod
```

## Step 2 -- Plan resource requests and limits by service, not by template

catalog-api's traffic is read-heavy and comparatively steady, so the plan sizes it with conservative, well-understood requests and limits and a modest baseline replica count -- it doesn't need to plan for sudden multi-times spikes the way checkout-api does. checkout-api sits behind cart submission and order placement, calls out to VoltPay on the critical path, and sees traffic that spikes hard around popular on-sales -- the plan sizes it with more headroom between request and limit, and flags it as the service that needs Horizontal Pod Autoscaler configuration so replica count can react to a real spike rather than being fixed.

```text
# planned sizing approach, exact numbers set once staging load data exists
catalog-api:   steady baseline, tight request/limit ratio, fixed-ish replica count
checkout-api:  spiky baseline, wider request/limit headroom, HPA-driven replica count
```

## Step 3 -- Plan the rollout strategy

A rolling update is planned for both services: new pods come up and must pass a readiness probe before Kubernetes routes traffic to them, and old pods are only terminated once enough new ones are confirmed ready. This avoids a hard cutover that could drop requests mid-flight -- a real concern for checkout-api specifically, since a dropped request there can mean an abandoned cart or an order submission that never completes, not just a slightly slower page load.

```text
# planned strategy, not yet encoded in a Deployment manifest
strategy: RollingUpdate
readiness probe: required before new pod receives traffic
old pod teardown: only after new pod is Ready
```

## Step 4 -- Plan the promotion path through environments

An image that has already cleared the CI/CD pipeline's lint/test and scan gate from the last lesson is planned to land in `dev` first, get validated there, promote to `staging` for a closer-to-production check against realistic data volumes, and only then promote to `prod`. The plan commits to this three-stage shape without yet fixing exactly what gate triggers each promotion -- an automated check, a manual approval, or some mix -- since that decision is better made once the monitoring plan in the next lesson exists to say what "healthy in staging" actually measures.

## Step 5 -- Flag what this plan intentionally leaves open

This lesson's plan deliberately does not fix exact CPU/memory numbers, does not fix the HPA's scaling thresholds, and does not fix what the readiness probe actually checks beyond "the service responds" -- all three depend on real traffic and monitoring data this project doesn't have yet. Marcus brings this environment-and-rollout plan to Ananya Reddy next, since the monitoring plan she helps build has to be able to observe exactly the environments and rollout behavior described here.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned three EKS namespaces (dev/staging/prod) holding both services, resource sizing split by traffic shape -- catalog-api steady/tight, checkout-api spiky with HPA headroom -- and a rolling-update strategy gated on readiness probes, promoted stage by stage. Exact resource numbers, HPA thresholds, and promotion gates are explicitly deferred pending real staging data and the monitoring plan.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned how our test, staging, and live environments will be structured, and how the two services get resourced differently since checkout traffic spikes much harder than catalog browsing does. We've also planned how new versions get rolled out without dropping in-progress requests. Nothing is built yet -- this plan feeds the next implementation steps.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned how the ticketing and checkout systems will run safely across testing, staging, and live environments, sized appropriately for the fact that checkout traffic spikes hard around popular events while browsing traffic stays steady, with a rollout approach designed so customers mid-purchase are never dropped when we ship an update.

lessons.title: Planning Monitoring and Alerting
lessons.summary: Planning the Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager monitoring approach for catalog-api and checkout-api, and fixing the stated goal that the team needs to know when customers can't actually complete a purchase, not just when a server returns an error code -- without yet locking in the exact alert-rule definitions.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the CI/CD pipeline and the Kubernetes environment both planned, Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy now plan how the team will actually know whether any of this is working once real traffic hits it. This lesson plans the monitoring approach in general terms: Prometheus scraping metrics from both services and the EKS cluster, Grafana dashboards built on top of those metrics, and Alertmanager routing alerts to Slack for day-to-day awareness and PagerDuty for anything that needs someone woken up.

The goal gets written down plainly in this lesson, as a stated requirement rather than an assumption: the team needs to know when customers can't actually complete a purchase, not just when a server returns an error code. This lesson plans the approach to that goal at a conceptual level -- what gets scraped, what gets dashboarded, and where alerts route -- without yet configuring a single alert rule. The first concrete alert, including exactly how "error" gets defined, is a decision for the implementation lesson that builds it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a lifeguard at a pool who only blows the whistle when someone is visibly splashing and yelling for help. That catches a lot of real trouble. But a far quieter kind of trouble -- someone who's quietly struggling and going under without making noise -- would never trigger that whistle at all, even though it's just as serious, maybe more so.

Marcus and Ananya are planning the pool's whole watch system here: where the lifeguard stands, what signals they're trained to watch for, and who gets called if something's wrong. They're writing down, out loud, that the real job is noticing when a swimmer is actually in trouble -- not just noticing loud splashing. But exactly how to catch every single quiet kind of trouble is still being worked out; this lesson plans the watch system in general and says plainly what it has to eventually catch, without claiming every edge case has already been solved.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The monitoring plan has three layers. Prometheus is planned to scrape metrics from catalog-api, checkout-api, and the EKS cluster itself -- request rates, latencies, pod resource usage, and HTTP response status codes at minimum. Grafana dashboards are planned on top of those metrics, giving the team and Celeste Marchbanks a visual read on both services' health. Alertmanager is planned to route alerts by severity: routine, actionable-but-not-urgent alerts to Slack, and anything that needs immediate human response to PagerDuty.

The goal Marcus and Ananya fix in writing, before any alert rule exists, is deliberately stronger than "the servers are up." Celeste's concern from the start of this project has been that Haverbrook Tickets needs to actually know when customers can't check out -- not just know when a server is throwing errors. A server returning healthy HTTP status codes while customers quietly fail to complete real purchases would still look fine on an infrastructure dashboard, which is exactly the gap this stated goal is written down to eventually close. Writing the goal down now, before any rule is configured, gives later lessons something concrete to measure the finished alerting against.

At the planning level, it's realistic -- and this plan says so directly -- that the first concrete alert the team builds will most likely be an HTTP-level error-rate alert: flagging when the proportion of non-2xx responses from either service crosses a threshold. That's a standard, well-understood starting point, and it will catch a large and real class of problems -- a crashing pod, a bad deploy, a database connection pool exhausted, EKS node pressure. This plan does not yet work through every edge case a payment-processing integration like checkout-api's VoltPay call might have in its own error-handling design, and it doesn't claim the monitoring approach has already been proven to catch every real failure mode a customer could experience. That honesty is deliberate: the implementation lesson that actually defines the first alert rule, and any lesson after it that validates monitoring against a real incident, are where that gets tested for real -- not assumed true here.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Plan what gets scraped

Prometheus is planned to scrape metrics from three sources: catalog-api, checkout-api, and the underlying EKS cluster (node and pod resource usage). At minimum, the plan calls for both services to expose request rate, request latency, and HTTP response status code as metrics Prometheus can scrape -- the baseline any HTTP-serving application is expected to expose.

```text
# planned scrape targets, not yet a running Prometheus config
scrape: catalog-api    -> request_rate, latency, http_status
scrape: checkout-api   -> request_rate, latency, http_status
scrape: eks cluster     -> node/pod cpu, memory, pod restarts
```

## Step 2 -- Plan the Grafana dashboards

One dashboard per service is planned, built on the scraped metrics above, giving Marcus, Ananya, and Lin Chao a visual view of each service's health day to day. A cluster-level dashboard is planned alongside them, covering the EKS environments built in the Kubernetes planning lesson. Celeste Marchbanks gets access to these dashboards directly, consistent with her stated interest in visibility into the system rather than secondhand status updates.

## Step 3 -- Plan the Alertmanager routing

Alertmanager is planned to route by severity rather than send everything to one place: alerts that are real but not urgent go to a Slack channel the team watches during work hours, and alerts serious enough to need an immediate human response route to PagerDuty. This two-tier routing is planned now so the implementation lesson that writes the first rules has somewhere real to send them.

```text
# planned routing shape
severity: warning   -> Slack
severity: critical  -> PagerDuty
```

## Step 4 -- Write down the real goal, before any rule exists

The plan fixes one requirement in writing: the team needs to know when customers can't actually complete a purchase, not just when a server returns an error code. This echoes Celeste's concern from early in this project -- that a system can look healthy on every infrastructure measure while real customers are quietly failing to buy tickets. Stating this goal now, before a single alert rule is configured, gives later validation work something specific to check the finished alerting against, rather than assuming any alert the team builds automatically satisfies it.

## Step 5 -- Be honest about what the plan commits to right now

The plan commits to one concrete starting point: the first alert the implementation lesson builds will most likely be an HTTP-level error-rate alert, watching for a rise in non-2xx responses from either service. That is a reasonable, standard first alert, and it will catch a large class of real problems. This plan does not yet walk through every integration's own error-handling behavior -- including how checkout-api's VoltPay integration reports a failed payment -- against that alert definition; that level of detail belongs to the implementation lesson that writes the actual rule, and to whatever validates it later against real traffic. Marcus and Ananya bring this monitoring plan, with the stated customer-facing goal and the two-tier routing, to Celeste for review before any rule gets written.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned Prometheus scrape targets (both services plus cluster metrics), per-service and cluster Grafana dashboards, and two-tier Alertmanager routing (Slack for warning, PagerDuty for critical). Fixed the explicit goal -- alert on real customer-facing checkout failure, not just HTTP error codes -- without yet configuring a rule; flagged that the first planned alert is HTTP-level error rate and that edge cases like a payment integration's own failure-handling are not yet walked through.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned how we'll monitor both systems -- dashboards the team and Celeste can see, and alerts that route to Slack or to an on-call page depending on severity. We've written down the real standard we're holding this to: knowing when customers actually can't complete a purchase, not just when a server reports an error. The first alert we build will likely start simple, with more refinement planned as we learn more.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned how we'll watch both systems once they're live, including making sure your team has visibility through dashboards, not just raw logs. We've written down the standard that matters most to you -- knowing when real customers can't finish buying a ticket, not just when a server technically reports an error. The first version of this monitoring will be a reasonable starting point, with room to get more precise as we learn from real usage.

lessons.title: Provisioning the Infrastructure with Terraform
lessons.summary: The first real implementation step -- writing the actual Terraform configuration for Haverbrook Tickets' AWS VPC, EKS cluster, the catalog-api and checkout-api Amazon ECR repositories, and the RDS Postgres instance that both services will eventually read from and write to.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Every planning lesson so far has pointed at this moment: Marcus Oyelaran opens a Terraform project and actually provisions the AWS infrastructure the rest of this implementation will run on. This lesson writes the real Terraform configuration for four pieces: a VPC sized for an EKS workload, the `haverbrook-tickets` EKS cluster with its `dev`/`staging`/`prod` namespaces created on top of it, two Amazon ECR repositories -- one for catalog-api, one for checkout-api -- and an RDS Postgres instance for application data.

This lesson is scoped to infrastructure only. No application code gets containerized here, no GitHub Actions workflow gets written, and no Kubernetes Deployment manifests get applied -- those are separate implementation lessons that need this infrastructure to already exist before they can target anything against it.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine building an actual building before anyone moves in a single piece of furniture: pouring the foundation, running the electrical and plumbing, building the loading dock, and putting in a secure storage room, all before a single desk or chair arrives. That's what this lesson does for Haverbrook Tickets -- it builds the real AWS foundation: a private network, a cluster of servers that will run the actual applications, two separate storage shelves for the finished, ready-to-run packages of each service, and a database to hold the real data.

Nobody is moving the catalog-api or checkout-api code in yet, and nobody is wiring up the pipeline that builds those packages. This lesson just pours the foundation and wires the building correctly, using Terraform instead of clicking around the AWS console by hand, so the exact same infrastructure can be rebuilt the same way every time.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson is pure infrastructure-as-code construction, executed in the dependency order Terraform and AWS actually require: the VPC and its subnets first, since everything else gets attached to them; the EKS cluster next, since it needs the VPC's subnets to place its nodes and control plane into; the ECR repositories, which are independent of the VPC and can be created in parallel; and the RDS Postgres instance last, since it depends on the VPC's subnets and a dedicated DB subnet group.

The VPC is planned with both public and private subnets across multiple Availability Zones -- public subnets for the NAT gateway and any internet-facing load balancer, private subnets for the EKS worker nodes and the RDS instance, keeping the database and application pods off the public internet by construction rather than by a firewall rule someone has to remember to add. The EKS cluster is provisioned with its control plane and a managed node group, sized as a starting point that the Kubernetes planning lesson's `dev`/`staging`/`prod` namespace plan will run inside -- namespaces are a Kubernetes-level construct created inside this one cluster, not three separate clusters, matching the namespace-isolation decision made in that planning lesson.

Two ECR repositories are created, one per service, matching the per-service repository the CI/CD planning lesson named as its push target -- `catalog-api` and `checkout-api` -- each with image scanning on push enabled as a second, always-on layer of vulnerability detection that complements, rather than replaces, the Trivy gate already planned into the pipeline itself.

The RDS Postgres instance is provisioned inside the VPC's private subnets only, with a security group that permits inbound traffic solely from the EKS node security group -- no direct internet exposure, no broad CIDR rule. This is the single database instance both catalog-api and checkout-api will eventually connect to once the implementation lessons ahead containerize them and wire up their connection strings; this lesson's job is only to make sure the instance, its subnet group, and its access boundary exist correctly before that wiring happens.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Provisioned the VPC (public/private subnets across 3 AZs), the haverbrook-tickets EKS cluster with a managed node group, two scan-on-push ECR repositories (catalog-api, checkout-api) with immutable tags, and an RDS Postgres instance locked to the EKS node security group in private subnets only. Containerization, CI/CD wiring, and Kubernetes manifests are explicitly out of scope for this step.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've built the actual cloud foundation everything else runs on: a secure network, the cluster that will run both applications, separate storage for each service's deployable packages, and the database. This is pure infrastructure; getting our actual application code running on top of it comes in the next steps.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've built the real cloud foundation for Haverbrook Tickets' new systems -- a secure network, the computing cluster that will run the ticketing site and checkout, and the database behind them -- all defined as code so it can be rebuilt identically if we ever need to. Everything else in this project gets built on top of what we just provisioned.

lessons.title: Containerizing catalog-api and checkout-api
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran writes production Dockerfiles for Haverbrook Tickets' two services -- the Node.js catalog-api and the Python/FastAPI checkout-api -- with multi-stage builds, non-root users, and health-check endpoints, then pushes both images to the Amazon ECR repositories Terraform provisioned in the last lesson.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With Terraform now provisioning the VPC, the Amazon EKS cluster, two Amazon ECR repositories, and the RDS Postgres instance, Marcus Oyelaran -- Haverbrook Tickets' DevOps/Platform Engineer -- has a cluster to deploy to and nowhere yet to deploy from. This lesson builds the missing piece: a real, production-grade Dockerfile for each of Haverbrook's two services, so both can be built into container images and pushed into the ECR repositories that are sitting there waiting.

**catalog-api** is a Node.js service that serves event and ticket-tier listings -- read-heavy, stateless, and the simpler of the two to containerize. **checkout-api** is a Python/FastAPI service that owns the shopping cart and order-submission flow; on submission, it calls out to Haverbrook's external payment processor, **VoltPay**, to actually charge the customer's card. Lin Chao's backend team already built and owns all of that application logic -- Marcus's job in this lesson is strictly the container packaging around it: a correct multi-stage Dockerfile, a non-root runtime user, a dedicated health-check endpoint separate from the service's business logic, and a clean push to each service's ECR repository, tagged and ready for the CI/CD pipeline the next lesson builds.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of a container image like a lunchbox you pack once so it travels the same way no matter where it goes -- onto the laptop you tested on, onto a teammate's machine, onto the real servers in AWS. If you just copy your project folder around, the lunchbox might be missing something, or it might be way bigger and messier than it needs to be, with tools nobody needs once the food -- the actual app -- is cooked and ready to eat.

That's what Marcus fixes in this lesson. For each of Haverbrook's two apps, he writes a recipe (a Dockerfile) with two stages: one messy kitchen where the app actually gets built, and one clean, small lunchbox that only has exactly what's needed to run it -- nothing extra, and never running as the kitchen's head chef (the all-powerful root user), just a regular trusted helper. Each lunchbox also gets a little window on the side -- a health-check endpoint -- so anyone outside can glance in and see 'yep, still breathing' without digging through everything inside.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A multi-stage Dockerfile is the standard answer to the two things that make container images slow, large, and riskier than they need to be: build-time tooling leaking into the runtime image, and a final image that ends up running as root with a much bigger attack surface than the application actually needs. For catalog-api, the build stage uses a `node` image to run `npm ci` and any build step, and the final stage copies only `node_modules` and the compiled application into a slim `node:20-alpine` runtime image, running as a dedicated non-root `node` user. For checkout-api, the build stage uses a `python` image to resolve dependencies into a virtual environment, and the final stage copies that resolved environment into a slim `python:3.12-slim` runtime image, running as a dedicated non-root `appuser`.

Both Dockerfiles expose a `/healthz` endpoint that Kubernetes will later use for liveness and readiness probes in Lesson 12 -- a deliberately separate, trivial endpoint that just confirms the process is up and able to serve traffic, distinct from the services' actual business routes. For checkout-api specifically, that separation matters: checkout-api's `/checkout` route is where Lin Chao's team's order-submission logic lives, including its call out to VoltPay to charge the customer. That existing application code -- built by Lin Chao's team well before this containerization work started -- already catches a VoltPay timeout or a declined card and returns a normal `HTTP 200` response with a JSON body such as `{"orderStatus": "failed", "reason": "payment_timeout"}`, specifically so the storefront's frontend treats a declined card as an ordinary, handled outcome rather than a server error. None of that changes here -- it's simply a fact about how checkout-api already behaves, worth noting while describing what the service does, because it shapes nothing about the Dockerfile itself. Both images get tagged and pushed to the two ECR repositories Terraform created in Lesson 8.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the ECR repositories are there

Marcus confirms the two repositories Terraform provisioned in the previous lesson:

```
aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names \
  haverbrook/catalog-api haverbrook/checkout-api --region us-east-1
```

Both repositories exist, empty, waiting for a first image.

## Step 2 -- Write the catalog-api Dockerfile (Node.js)

```dockerfile
# ---- build stage ----
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev=false
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# ---- runtime stage ----
FROM node:20-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S catalog -G appgroup
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package*.json ./
USER catalog
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/healthz || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

`catalog-api` exposes a lightweight `GET /healthz` route that returns `200 OK` with `{"status": "ok"}` -- nothing touches the database or any downstream service, so the health check can't be dragged down by something unrelated going slow.

## Step 3 -- Write the checkout-api Dockerfile (Python/FastAPI)

```dockerfile
# ---- build stage ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv \
  && /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

# ---- runtime stage ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash appuser
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz')" || exit 1
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

checkout-api owns the cart and order-submission flow, and its `POST /checkout` route is where Lin Chao's team's existing integration with Haverbrook's payment processor, **VoltPay**, runs. As with `/healthz` on catalog-api, checkout-api's `/healthz` route is a separate, minimal endpoint -- it answers 'is the process up,' not 'did the last order succeed' -- which is exactly how Lin Chao's team already built checkout-api to behave: when VoltPay times out or declines a card, the application catches that case and returns `HTTP 200` with a body like `{"orderStatus": "failed", "reason": "payment_timeout"}`, so a declined card reads as a handled business outcome to the frontend rather than a server error. That's existing behavior Marcus is simply packaging here, not something this containerization work changes.

## Step 4 -- Build and tag both images locally

```bash
docker build -t catalog-api:local ./catalog-api
docker build -t checkout-api:local ./checkout-api
```

## Step 5 -- Authenticate to ECR and push

```bash
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | \
  docker login --username AWS --password-stdin \
  <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com

docker tag catalog-api:local \
  <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/haverbrook/catalog-api:v0.1.0
docker tag checkout-api:local \
  <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/haverbrook/checkout-api:v0.1.0

docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/haverbrook/catalog-api:v0.1.0
docker push <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/haverbrook/checkout-api:v0.1.0
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm with the team

Marcus confirms both images in ECR with Celeste Marchbanks and Lin Chao: both services build cleanly, run as non-root, expose a working health-check route separate from their business logic, and are ready for the CI/CD pipeline that the next lesson automates. Lin Chao confirms checkout-api's container starts and serves traffic identically to how it runs in her team's local development environment -- the VoltPay integration and its existing payment-failure handling are unchanged, exactly as expected from a packaging exercise.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Wrote multi-stage Dockerfiles for both services: catalog-api on node:20-alpine, checkout-api on python:3.12-slim, both running as dedicated non-root users with a separate /healthz endpoint for container health checks. Confirmed checkout-api's existing VoltPay integration and its catch-and-return-200 handling for timeouts/declines carries over unchanged into the container. Both images tagged with v0.1.0 and pushed to the ECR repositories from Lesson 8.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Both services are now packaged as container images and sitting in our container registry, ready for the CI/CD pipeline we build next. No application behavior changed in this step -- this was purely about packaging the existing code so it can run reliably in AWS.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Both of our core services are now packaged in a standard, portable format and stored in AWS, ready to be deployed automatically. This is the foundation that lets us ship changes quickly and consistently going forward.

lessons.title: Building the CI/CD Pipeline in GitHub Actions
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran builds the GitHub Actions workflow that lints and tests every pull request, builds a container image, blocks on any critical vulnerability found by a Trivy scan, tags the image with the git commit SHA, and pushes it to Amazon ECR to trigger deployment.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
catalog-api and checkout-api can now be built into container images by hand and pushed to Amazon ECR -- but 'by hand' doesn't scale past the first push, and it gives nobody confidence that a change is safe before it ships. This lesson replaces that manual process with a real GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline: one workflow, triggered on every pull request and every merge to `main`, that lints and tests the code, builds the container image, scans it for known vulnerabilities, and -- only if all of that passes -- tags the image with the exact git commit SHA and pushes it to the correct ECR repository.

The design decision Marcus makes here is where to put the safety gate. Linting and unit tests run on every pull request, giving Lin Chao and the rest of the backend team fast feedback before anything merges. The container build and the vulnerability scan -- using **Trivy**, an open-source scanner -- run after merge to `main`, and the scan is configured to fail the build outright on any **critical**-severity finding, not just report it. Only an image that passes the scan gets tagged with its git SHA and pushed to ECR, where it becomes available for the staged EKS rollout built in Lesson 12. Celeste Marchbanks gets exactly what she asked a DevOps project to deliver: nothing reaches a running environment without passing the same automated checks, every single time.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a bakery that used to let any finished loaf of bread go straight into the display case, because someone remembered to check it was good -- most of the time. This lesson builds an assembly line instead: every batch of dough gets tasted and checked automatically the moment it's mixed, then baked, then run through a metal detector before it's ever allowed near the display case. If the metal detector finds something seriously wrong, that loaf simply doesn't go out -- no one has to remember to catch it, because the line itself won't let it pass.

That's the pipeline Marcus builds for Haverbrook Tickets. Every proposed code change gets automatically tested the moment someone opens it for review. Once it's approved and merged, the code gets baked into a container image, and that image gets scanned for known security problems. If the scan finds something serious, the pipeline stops right there -- nothing with a serious known flaw is allowed to move on toward the real servers.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This workflow is deliberately split into two jobs with two different triggers, because pull-request feedback and deployment-image production have different speed and safety requirements. The `test` job runs on `pull_request`, installing dependencies and running each service's linter and unit test suite -- fast, cheap, and giving Lin Chao's team a signal before a human reviewer even looks at the diff. The `build-scan-push` job runs on `push` to `main`, after a pull request has already been reviewed and merged, and is where the actual deployment artifact gets produced.

Inside `build-scan-push`, the image is built with `docker build`, then scanned in place with `aquasecurity/trivy-action`, configured with `exit-code: '1'` and `severity: 'CRITICAL'` -- meaning the GitHub Actions job itself fails, and nothing downstream runs, the moment Trivy finds even one unpatched critical CVE in the image's OS packages or application dependencies. Only after the scan step exits cleanly does the workflow compute the tag -- `${{ github.sha }}`, the exact seven-or-more-character (here, full) commit SHA that produced this image, which makes every image in ECR traceable back to the exact commit that built it -- log in to ECR using the `aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login` action, and push. The workflow finishes by invoking a deployment trigger (a `workflow_dispatch` call to the deploy workflow built out in Lesson 12), rather than deploying directly from this file, which keeps the build/scan/push concerns cleanly separate from the staged-rollout concerns.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Lay out the two jobs

Marcus creates `.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml` at the repo root, covering both `catalog-api` and `checkout-api` with a matrix strategy so one workflow file serves both services.

```yaml
name: CI/CD

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        service: [catalog-api, checkout-api]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Lint and test catalog-api (Node)
        if: matrix.service == 'catalog-api'
        working-directory: catalog-api
        run: |
          npm ci
          npm run lint
          npm test -- --ci
      - name: Lint and test checkout-api (Python)
        if: matrix.service == 'checkout-api'
        working-directory: checkout-api
        run: |
          python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
          ruff check .
          pytest -q
```

## Step 2 -- Build, scan, and gate on critical vulnerabilities

```yaml
  build-scan-push:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        service: [catalog-api, checkout-api]
    permissions:
      id-token: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build image
        run: |
          docker build -t ${{ matrix.service }}:${{ github.sha }} ./${{ matrix.service }}

      - name: Scan image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@0.24.0
        with:
          image-ref: ${{ matrix.service }}:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: CRITICAL
          exit-code: '1'
          ignore-unfixed: true
```

```
MARCUS: ignore-unfixed is on, because failing a build over a CVE
        with no available patch just blocks shipping and teaches
        everyone to ignore the scanner. A critical finding with a
        real fix available stops the build, every time.
```

## Step 3 -- Tag with the git SHA and push to ECR

```yaml
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/github-actions-ecr-push
          aws-region: us-east-1

      - name: Login to Amazon ECR
        id: ecr-login
        uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2

      - name: Tag and push
        env:
          REGISTRY: ${{ steps.ecr-login.outputs.registry }}
        run: |
          docker tag ${{ matrix.service }}:${{ github.sha }} \
            $REGISTRY/haverbrook/${{ matrix.service }}:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push $REGISTRY/haverbrook/${{ matrix.service }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

## Step 4 -- Hand off to deployment

```yaml
      - name: Trigger staged deployment
        uses: peter-evans/repository-dispatch@v3
        with:
          event-type: deploy-to-dev
          client-payload: '{"service": "${{ matrix.service }}", "sha": "${{ github.sha }}"}'
```

This dispatches to the staged-rollout workflow built in Lesson 12 -- `dev`, then `staging`, then a manual approval gate, then `prod` -- keeping build/scan/push fully separate from the deployment mechanics.

## Step 5 -- Confirm with the team

Marcus opens a throwaway pull request against `checkout-api` to confirm the `test` job runs and passes, then merges to `main` and confirms `build-scan-push` runs end to end: image builds, Trivy scan passes clean, image lands in ECR tagged with the real commit SHA, and the deploy-trigger fires. He walks Celeste Marchbanks through the gate directly:

```
MARCUS:   Nothing reaches a running environment without passing
          lint, tests, and a vulnerability scan first. If Trivy
          finds a critical, fixable CVE, the pipeline stops there --
          it doesn't get a vote on whether to continue.

CELESTE:  That's exactly the guardrail I wanted in place before we
          start deploying to production regularly.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a two-job GitHub Actions workflow: a pull_request-triggered test job (lint + unit tests per service via a matrix strategy), and a push-to-main-triggered build-scan-push job that builds the image, runs a Trivy scan with exit-code 1 on CRITICAL severity (ignore-unfixed enabled), tags the image with the full git SHA, and pushes to the matching ECR repository via OIDC-assumed role. A repository_dispatch event hands off to the staged-rollout workflow.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have a fully automated pipeline: every proposed change gets tested automatically, and every merged change gets scanned for serious security vulnerabilities before it can move toward deployment. Nothing bypasses this -- it's the same check every time, for every change.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Code changes to our ticketing platform now go through an automatic safety check before they can be deployed, including a security scan that blocks anything with a serious known vulnerability. This reduces the risk of a mistake or a known security issue reaching our customers.

lessons.title: Setting Up Prometheus, Grafana, and the Error-Rate Alert
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran and SRE Ananya Reddy stand up Prometheus scraping and a Grafana dashboard for both services, then build and test a production error-rate alert in Alertmanager -- defining an error as any non-2xx HTTP status code from checkout-api -- and confirm it fires correctly against a simulated 500.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Haverbrook Tickets' two services are now building, scanning, and shipping through a real pipeline -- but nobody can see how they're actually behaving once they're running. This lesson closes that gap: Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy, Haverbrook's SRE, stand up **Prometheus** to scrape metrics from both `catalog-api` and `checkout-api`, build a **Grafana** dashboard covering request rate, latency, and error rate for each service, and configure **Alertmanager** to page the on-call engineer when checkout-api's error rate crosses a defined threshold.

The core of this lesson is that error-rate alert, and Marcus and Ananya build it the way most teams do: they define an 'error' as any HTTP response from checkout-api with a status code outside the 2xx range -- a standard, textbook definition, expressed as a straightforward PromQL ratio over the `http_requests_total` counter, broken out by `status`. They test it the way most teams test an alert like this: by deliberately triggering a real `500 Internal Server Error` in a non-production environment and confirming Alertmanager fires and pages correctly. It does, cleanly, on the first try. Both engineers walk away satisfied that the alert does exactly what it was built to do -- flag checkout-api when something is going wrong.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine putting a smoke detector in a kitchen. The obvious thing to make it react to is smoke -- and that's exactly what Marcus and Ananya build here: a detector that sounds an alarm whenever checkout-api sends back a response that isn't a normal, healthy 'everything's fine' answer. To make sure the detector actually works, they hold a candle under it on purpose -- they cause a real, ordinary kind of problem (a server error) -- and sure enough, the alarm goes off exactly like it's supposed to.

That's a completely reasonable way to build and test a smoke detector. It reacts to smoke, and it was tested with smoke, and it worked. Whether there's some other kind of problem this particular detector wouldn't notice isn't something this lesson looks into -- the detector does precisely what it was designed and tested to do.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Prometheus is configured with a standard scrape config targeting each service's `/metrics` endpoint on a 15-second interval, and both catalog-api and checkout-api expose request-count and latency histograms through each language's respective client library -- `prom-client` for the Node.js catalog-api, `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` for the Python/FastAPI checkout-api. The Grafana dashboard built on top covers the standard trio for each service: request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, and error rate, giving Ananya a real-time operational view she didn't have before this lesson.

The production alert is the meaningful deliverable, and it's built the way almost every team builds a first error-rate alert: against the HTTP status code, because that's the signal every web framework and every load balancer already exposes without any additional application-level work. The PromQL expression is a ratio of non-2xx requests to total requests over a rolling window:

```
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api"}[5m]))
> 0.02
```

That query, and the alert rule built on it, is genuinely well-constructed: it uses a rate over a rolling window rather than a raw counter (so it isn't skewed by traffic volume), it's scoped to checkout-api specifically rather than averaged across both services, and the 2% threshold was discussed and agreed with Ananya as a reasonable bar above normal background noise. Marcus and Ananya validate it the standard way -- deploying a deliberate `raise HTTPException(status_code=500)` to a non-prod checkout-api instance and confirming the rate crosses 2%, Alertmanager fires, and the configured Slack/PagerDuty route receives it. It does, within the expected evaluation window, and both engineers sign off on the alert as working correctly. Nothing in this lesson asks how checkout-api represents a *declined payment* at the HTTP layer -- that's a question about a completely different part of the system, outside the scope of building and validating an HTTP-status-based error-rate alert.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Expose metrics from both services

```javascript
// catalog-api: metrics middleware
const client = require('prom-client');
const httpRequestsTotal = new client.Counter({
  name: 'http_requests_total',
  help: 'Total HTTP requests',
  labelNames: ['service', 'route', 'method', 'status'],
});
app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {
  res.set('Content-Type', client.register.contentType);
  res.end(await client.register.metrics());
});
```

```python
# checkout-api: FastAPI instrumentation
from prometheus_fastapi_instrumentator import Instrumentator

Instrumentator().instrument(app).expose(app, endpoint="/metrics")
```

## Step 2 -- Configure Prometheus to scrape both services

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: catalog-api
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
        regex: catalog-api
        action: keep
    metrics_path: /metrics

  - job_name: checkout-api
    kubernetes_sd_configs:
      - role: pod
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app]
        regex: checkout-api
        action: keep
    metrics_path: /metrics
```

## Step 3 -- Build the Grafana dashboard

Ananya builds one Grafana dashboard with three panels per service: request rate (`sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="$service"}[5m])) by (route)`), latency percentiles (`histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="$service"}[5m]))`), and error rate (the same ratio used in the alert, graphed over time rather than thresholded).

## Step 4 -- Define and build the error-rate alert

```yaml
# checkout-api-alerts.yml (Prometheus rule file)
groups:
  - name: checkout-api.rules
    rules:
      - alert: CheckoutApiHighErrorRate
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api"}[5m]))
          > 0.02
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          service: checkout-api
        annotations:
          summary: "checkout-api error rate above 2% for 5+ minutes"
          description: "Non-2xx response rate on checkout-api has exceeded 2% over a 5 minute window."
```

```
ANANYA:  I want this scoped to checkout-api specifically, not blended
         with catalog-api's traffic -- checkout failures are the ones
         that actually cost us orders.

MARCUS:  Agreed. Non-2xx over a 5-minute rate window, 2% threshold,
         sustained for 5 minutes before it pages -- that should catch
         a real problem without paging someone over a routine blip.
```

## Step 5 -- Route the alert in Alertmanager

```yaml
# alertmanager.yml
route:
  receiver: oncall-pagerduty
  routes:
    - match:
        service: checkout-api
        severity: critical
      receiver: oncall-pagerduty
      group_wait: 30s

receivers:
  - name: oncall-pagerduty
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: <pagerduty-integration-key>
```

## Step 6 -- Test it against a real 500

In the `staging` namespace, Marcus temporarily deploys a build of checkout-api with a forced `raise HTTPException(status_code=500)` on a test route, then drives traffic against it.

```
ANANYA:  Error rate panel just crossed 2% on the dashboard. Watching
         for the page now.

MARCUS:  Alertmanager fired right at the five-minute mark, and
         PagerDuty has it. That's exactly the behavior we wanted.
```

The alert fires correctly, pages on-call as configured, and resolves automatically once the forced-error build is rolled back and the error rate drops.

## Step 7 -- Sign off

Marcus and Ananya document the alert -- definition, threshold, test method, and result -- as a working, validated production alert and move on to the staged EKS rollout in the next lesson. Ananya signs off that checkout-api now has real-time error visibility where there was none before.

```
ANANYA:  Dashboard's live, the alert fired exactly when we expected
         it to, and PagerDuty routing is confirmed. I'm comfortable
         calling this production-ready.

MARCUS:  Same here -- clean test, clean signal, reasonable
         threshold. I'll document the PromQL and the test steps so
         anyone on the team can see exactly how this was validated.
```

The alert, the dashboard, and the scrape configuration all go into the runbook Marcus keeps for the on-call rotation, alongside the PagerDuty routing key and escalation policy, so the next engineer on call has everything needed to respond the moment this alert fires again.

lessons.title: Deploying to EKS With a Staged Rollout
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran wires the CI/CD pipeline to a staged Kubernetes rollout -- dev, then staging, then a manual approval gate, then prod -- using a rolling-update strategy with readiness probes for both catalog-api and checkout-api on the EKS cluster from Lesson 8.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Images are building, scanning clean, and landing in ECR; Prometheus and Grafana can see what's running. This lesson closes the loop by actually deploying both services onto the **Amazon EKS** cluster Terraform provisioned in Lesson 8, through the three namespaces already set up there -- `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` -- in that order, with a human checkpoint before anything reaches production.

Marcus builds a Kubernetes Deployment and Service manifest for each of catalog-api and checkout-api, using a `RollingUpdate` strategy with `maxUnavailable: 0` so capacity never drops during a deploy, and readiness probes hitting each service's `/healthz` endpoint from Lesson 9 so Kubernetes never routes traffic to a pod that isn't actually ready. The GitHub Actions pipeline from Lesson 10 deploys automatically to `dev` on every successful build, automatically promotes to `staging` once `dev` passes its own smoke check, and then stops and waits for a named human -- Celeste Marchbanks or Marcus himself -- to click approve in GitHub's environment-protection UI before anything touches `prod`. The whole thing runs cleanly end to end on the first real test, and the team is satisfied with how smoothly both services move through all three environments.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about moving into a brand-new apartment. You wouldn't bring every box in through the front door and immediately start unpacking in the middle of the living room while people are already living there. You'd set boxes down in the hallway first (dev), check nothing's broken (staging), and then -- because this is the apartment people actually live in -- someone has to say 'okay, bring it in' (the approval gate) before anything actually gets carried into the living room (prod). And even then, you carry boxes in one at a time, never emptying the whole hallway into the living room all at once, so there's always a working living room the whole time.

That's exactly what Marcus builds here. Every new version of Haverbrook's two services moves through a hallway (dev), then a waiting room (staging), then waits for a real person to say go, before it finally reaches the living room (prod) -- and even in prod, it swaps in gradually, a few pods at a time, so customers are always being served by a working version.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The deployment manifests use a standard `RollingUpdate` strategy with `maxUnavailable: 0` and `maxSurge: 1`, meaning Kubernetes always spins up one additional new-version pod before it ever removes an old-version pod -- capacity never dips during a rollout, which matters for checkout-api given Haverbrook's spiky event-driven traffic. Readiness probes against `/healthz` (built in Lesson 9) gate when the Service's endpoint list actually includes a new pod, and liveness probes on the same endpoint let Kubernetes restart a pod that's stopped responding entirely, independent of whether it's ready for traffic.

The staged promotion itself is modeled as three GitHub Actions environments -- `dev`, `staging`, `prod` -- each mapped to the matching EKS namespace via `kubectl` context and `-n <namespace>`. Promotion from `dev` to `staging` is automatic, gated only by a scripted smoke check (`curl` against each service's `/healthz` and one real read-path endpoint) passing inside `dev`. Promotion from `staging` to `prod` is gated by a GitHub **environment protection rule** requiring a named reviewer's approval -- Celeste Marchbanks as business sponsor or Marcus as the engineer on call -- which pauses the workflow run entirely until someone approves it in the GitHub UI. This is a deliberate, standard safety control, separate from and unrelated to the monitoring and alerting work in the previous lesson: it's about controlling *when* a change reaches production, not about detecting what happens once it's there. The team runs a full real promotion -- a genuine version bump to catalog-api -- end to end through all three namespaces during this lesson, and it completes cleanly with no rollback needed.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the EKS namespaces

```bash
kubectl get namespaces
# dev, staging, prod -- all present from the Lesson 8 Terraform apply
```

## Step 2 -- Write the Deployment manifest (checkout-api, used as the template for both)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: checkout-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: checkout-api
          image: <account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/haverbrook/checkout-api:${IMAGE_TAG}
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: checkout-api
  namespace: dev
spec:
  selector:
    app: checkout-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

catalog-api gets the identical shape, pointed at port 3000 and its own ECR image. Both manifests are templated with Helm so the same chart deploys to `dev`, `staging`, and `prod` with only the namespace and replica count varying per environment.

## Step 3 -- Wire the GitHub Actions environments

```yaml
  deploy-dev:
    needs: build-scan-push
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: dev
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to dev
        run: |
          helm upgrade --install ${{ matrix.service }} ./charts/${{ matrix.service }} \
            --namespace dev --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Smoke check
        run: ./scripts/smoke-check.sh dev ${{ matrix.service }}

  deploy-staging:
    needs: deploy-dev
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - run: |
          helm upgrade --install ${{ matrix.service }} ./charts/${{ matrix.service }} \
            --namespace staging --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }}

  deploy-prod:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod   # <-- protection rule requires manual approval
    steps:
      - run: |
          helm upgrade --install ${{ matrix.service }} ./charts/${{ matrix.service }} \
            --namespace prod --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }}
```

## Step 4 -- Configure the manual approval gate on `prod`

In the GitHub repo settings, Marcus configures the `prod` environment with a required reviewer:

```
Settings -> Environments -> prod -> Required reviewers: Celeste Marchbanks, Marcus Oyelaran
```

The `deploy-prod` job now pauses and waits for one of them to click Approve before `helm upgrade` runs against the `prod` namespace.

## Step 5 -- Run a real promotion end to end

Marcus merges a genuine, small catalog-api version bump and watches it move through the pipeline:

```
MARCUS:   Dev deployed and smoke-checked clean in under a minute.
          Staging deployed right behind it, also clean. Prod is
          sitting at the approval gate now.

CELESTE:  Approving now -- looks good. Deployed?

MARCUS:   Rolling update is running -- one new pod up before the
          first old one comes down, zero dip in available replicas
          the whole way through. All three prod replicas are on the
          new version now.
```

## Step 6 -- Sign off

The rollout completes cleanly through all three namespaces with no rollback required. Marcus documents the Helm chart, the environment-gate configuration, and this first real promotion as the standard deployment path going forward, and the team -- satisfied with how smoothly it went -- turns its attention to the next phase of the build.
