Wired GitHub Actions environments (dev, staging, prod) to the matching EKS namespaces, with automatic dev-to-staging promotion gated on a smoke check and a required-reviewer protection rule gating staging-to-prod. Ran a full real promotion end to end with zero rollback.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Both services now deploy automatically through dev and staging, with a required human approval before anything reaches production. We ran a real deployment through the full pipeline today and it went smoothly from start to finish, with no issues.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We now have an automated, controlled process for releasing updates to our ticketing platform -- changes are tested in two earlier environments first, and a person has to explicitly approve anything before it reaches the production system our customers use. Today's first real run went cleanly.

lessons.title: Load-Testing Before Go-Live
lessons.summary: Before cutting over any real customer traffic, Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy load-test checkout-api and the browse/catalog service against a simulated ticket-on-sale traffic spike -- checking autoscaling, resource limits, pipeline behavior, and whether the error-rate alert actually pages someone when it should.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Haverbrook Tickets' worst traffic days aren't average days -- they're the ten minutes after a major act announces a show, when hundreds of thousands of fans hit "buy" at once. Before any of this new AWS/EKS infrastructure touches real customers, Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy need proof it survives that moment, not just a quiet Tuesday afternoon.

This lesson builds a k6 load-testing suite that models a realistic on-sale traffic shape against the `staging` EKS cluster, which is sized and configured identically to `prod`: a slow ramp as fans start refreshing the page, a sharp spike as the sale opens, and a sustained plateau as the queue drains. While that traffic runs, Marcus watches the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler add `checkout-api` and catalog-service pods in Grafana, confirms CPU and memory stay inside the resource requests and limits Terraform provisioned, and checks that GitHub Actions can still ship a routine deploy without dropping in-flight requests.

The second half of the test is just as important as the performance numbers: Ananya injects real, controlled HTTP 500 responses into a slice of checkout-api's staging traffic and confirms the production error-rate alert built in an earlier lesson doesn't just light up a Grafana panel -- it fires in Prometheus, routes through Alertmanager, and actually pages the on-call rotation within the expected window. A load test that proves the system is fast but never proves the alert wakes anyone up isn't a load test Marcus trusts. Every check in this lesson comes back green, and the team signs off to proceed to the real go-live.
lessons.explainSimple:
Before a new bridge opens to real traffic, engineers drive heavy trucks across it first -- not because they expect it to fail, but because "it held up on a calm day" and "it holds up during rush hour" are two completely different claims, and only one of them is the one that matters.

Marcus and Ananya do the same thing with a pretend rush hour: a flood of fake shoppers hitting the ticket site all at once, built by a tool that can generate hundreds of thousands of fake clicks on command. While the fake rush hour is happening, they watch whether the system adds more workers to keep up, whether it runs out of memory, and whether a routine software update can still go out safely in the middle of all that traffic.

Then they do something extra: they deliberately make a small slice of the pretend traffic fail on purpose, like pulling a fire alarm during a drill, just to make sure the alarm actually rings somewhere a real person will hear it -- not just that a light turns red on a screen nobody's watching.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Load testing against a plausible traffic shape, rather than a flat synthetic ramp, is the detail that makes this test worth trusting. Ticket on-sale traffic isn't steady-state load -- it's a thundering-herd spike with a long tail, and that shape stresses autoscaling lag, connection pool exhaustion, and cold-start latency in ways a smooth ramp never will. Modeling it in k6 against a `staging` cluster that mirrors `prod`'s node group sizing, HPA thresholds, and resource requests/limits is what makes the pass/fail criteria meaningful rather than theoretical.

The pipeline check matters for a reason that's easy to overlook: a load test that only proves steady-state capacity says nothing about what happens when a routine GitHub Actions deploy rolls a new pod version in the middle of peak traffic. Verifying readiness probes gate traffic correctly during a rolling update, under load, is what actually derisks "we can still ship code safely on a big sale day."

The fault-injection half of this test reflects a specific discipline: an alert is not validated by confirming its query is syntactically correct or its dashboard panel renders -- it's validated by proving the exact failure condition it's meant to catch actually reaches a human being, end to end, through Alertmanager's routing and paging integration, within the window the on-call runbook promises. Marcus and Ananya treat that as a release gate with the same seriousness as a latency SLO, because an alert that's never been proven to fire is, for practical purposes, a bet rather than a safeguard. The one caveat worth sitting with: this test proves the alert catches the failure mode it was built to detect. It says nothing about failure modes the alert wasn't built to detect -- that's a different kind of risk, caught differently, if it's caught at all.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Model the real traffic shape, not a flat ramp

Marcus and Ananya build a k6 script that mirrors how an actual Haverbrook Tickets on-sale behaves: a slow refresh-and-wait ramp, a sharp spike at sale-open, and a sustained plateau as the queue works through.

```javascript
// k6/onsale-spike.js
export const options = {
  stages: [
    { duration: "3m", target: 500 },    // fans refreshing before the drop
    { duration: "30s", target: 8000 },  // the drop -- sharp spike
    { duration: "10m", target: 6000 },  // sustained plateau, queue draining
    { duration: "3m", target: 0 },      // tail-off
  ],
  thresholds: {
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<800", "p(99)<1500"],
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],
  },
};
```

The test hits the real user flow -- browse, select seats, checkout -- against `staging`, which Terraform keeps sized identically to `prod`: same EKS node group instance types, same `checkout-api` resource requests/limits, same Horizontal Pod Autoscaler thresholds.

## Step 2 -- Watch autoscaling and resource headroom in Grafana

While the spike runs, Marcus watches the HPA add pods and confirms nothing is starved or throttled:

```
HPA events, checkout-api (staging) -- onsale-spike run
  t+0:00   replicas: 4   (baseline)
  t+3:05   replicas: 9   (CPU > 70% target, scaling triggered)
  t+3:40   replicas: 18  (spike absorbed)
  t+13:30  replicas: 7   (plateau drains, scaling down)

  Peak CPU/pod: 78% of limit  -- no throttling observed
  Peak memory/pod: 61% of limit -- no OOMKilled events
```

No pod restarts, no throttling, no evictions. Resource requests and limits set in Terraform give the HPA enough headroom to react before saturation.

## Step 3 -- Confirm the CI/CD pipeline survives a deploy under load

Ananya kicks off a routine GitHub Actions deploy of a trivial checkout-api change while the spike test is still running, to confirm the rolling update doesn't drop traffic:

```
GitHub Actions: deploy checkout-api v1.14.2 to staging
  Rolling update strategy: maxUnavailable=0, maxSurge=25%
  Readiness probe: /healthz, gates traffic until ready
  Result: 0 failed requests attributable to the rollout
          0 dropped connections during pod replacement
```

## Step 4 -- Inject a real failure and prove the alert actually pages someone

This is the part Marcus treats as non-negotiable. A dashboard that turns red is not the same thing as a human being getting paged. Using a staging-only feature flag already built into checkout-api for testing (`FORCE_ERROR_RATE_PCT`), Ananya forces 8% of staging requests to return a real HTTP 500:

```
# staging config override, 10-minute window
FORCE_ERROR_RATE_PCT=8
```

The error-rate alert, built in an earlier lesson, watches exactly this:

```promql
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api", status=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout-api"}[5m]))
> 0.02
```

```
ALERT: CheckoutApiHighErrorRate
  Fired: 4m50s after FORCE_ERROR_RATE_PCT applied
  Routed: Alertmanager -> #devops-oncall-staging
  Paged: on-call engineer notified via PagerDuty, ack'd in 1m20s
  Cleared: 3m after flag reset to 0
```

The alert fires, routes, and pages inside the expected window, exactly as designed.

## Step 5 -- Sign off

```
LOAD TEST SIGN-OFF -- onsale-spike.js, staging == prod sizing
  p95 latency: 640ms (threshold 800ms)  PASS
  Error rate under load: 0.3% (threshold 1%)  PASS
  HPA scale-up time: 40s to absorb spike  PASS
  Pipeline deploy under load: 0 dropped requests  PASS
  Alert fire-and-page (injected 500s): 4m50s to page  PASS
  Status: Cleared for go-live.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran a k6 spike test modeling real on-sale traffic against staging (sized identically to prod): HPA scaled checkout-api from 4 to 18 pods with no throttling or OOM events, a routine GitHub Actions deploy completed under load with zero dropped requests, and injecting a real 8% HTTP 500 rate confirmed the CheckoutApiHighErrorRate alert fires, routes through Alertmanager, and pages on-call within 5 minutes. All thresholds passed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We stress-tested the new infrastructure against a simulated ticket on-sale rush before touching real customers, including deliberately breaking a slice of it on purpose to confirm our alerting actually pages someone. Everything passed cleanly, and we're cleared to move to the real go-live.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We tested the new platform against the kind of traffic spike a hit show's on-sale actually creates, and it held up -- the system scaled automatically, stayed fast, and our alerting proved it can catch and page the team on a real problem. We're ready for launch.

lessons.title: Going Live
lessons.summary: Celeste Marchbanks gives the go/no-go call, and Marcus Oyelaran leads a staged cutover of real Haverbrook Tickets customer traffic onto the new AWS/EKS infrastructure -- a clean, uneventful launch with dashboards green from the first minute.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything up to this point -- the Terraform-provisioned AWS infrastructure, the containerized checkout-api and catalog-service, the GitHub Actions pipeline, the EKS rollout across dev/staging/prod, the Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager stack, and last lesson's load test -- has been building toward one moment: real Haverbrook Tickets customers, real ticket purchases, running on the new platform instead of the old one.

This lesson is that cutover. Marcus Oyelaran runs the team through a final go-live checklist with Celeste Marchbanks, who owns the go/no-go decision as business sponsor: infrastructure health, pipeline status, monitoring coverage, rollback plan, and support readiness all have to be a clean yes before anyone touches production traffic. Oscar Bennett's support team gets a short briefing beforehand so they know what's changing and who to call if something looks unusual in the first hours.

Rather than flipping every customer over at once, Marcus executes a staged cutover -- 10% of real traffic, then 50%, then 100% -- watching Grafana at each step before increasing the share, with a tested rollback plan ready the entire time. The team picks an off-peak window deliberately, to keep the blast radius small if anything does go wrong. It doesn't. Traffic ramps cleanly through all three stages, latency and error-rate dashboards stay nominal throughout, and Haverbrook Tickets is fully live on the new AWS/EKS platform by the end of the lesson -- a calm, well-executed launch with no sign yet of what's coming in the next one.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about how a city opens a brand-new bridge. Even after months of testing, nobody closes the old bridge and sends every single car across the new one at the same instant. They open one lane first, watch how it handles real traffic for a while, then open a second lane, then finally close the old bridge for good -- so if something unexpected happens, only a little bit of traffic is affected, and it's easy to send cars back to the old bridge.

Marcus does the same thing with Haverbrook Tickets' real customers. First just a small slice of real shoppers go through the new system while everyone else still uses the old one. Nothing breaks, so a bit more traffic moves over. Then more. Then, once everyone's confident, all of it. The whole time, there's a boss -- Celeste -- whose job is to give the final "yes, go" before any of it starts, and a support team standing by in case customers notice anything strange. Nobody does. It just works.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A staged percentage-based cutover, rather than an all-at-once switch, is the standard way to control blast radius on a migration this consequential -- a 500K-MAU marketplace moving its checkout path off legacy infrastructure. Ramping real traffic through 10%, 50%, and 100% stages, with a deliberate observation window at each stage before increasing the share, converts an irreversible, all-or-nothing event into a series of small, individually reversible decisions. If the 10% stage had shown elevated latency or error rate, the rollback -- shifting weight back to the legacy path -- would have cost a small fraction of customers a brief inconvenience rather than a platform-wide outage.

The go/no-go checklist format matters organizationally as much as technically: it forces every workstream -- infrastructure, pipeline, monitoring, support readiness -- to independently certify "ready" before Celeste Marchbanks, as business sponsor, authorizes the cutover, rather than leaving go-live as an implicit default that happens if nobody objects. Briefing Oscar Bennett's support team beforehand closes a gap that's easy to miss on a purely technical rollout: the people fielding customer contact need to know a migration happened before they're diagnosing symptoms of it blind.

Choosing an off-peak window for the cutover itself, independent of the staged ramp, is a second, complementary layer of risk reduction -- it ensures that even the smallest stage of the ramp isn't absorbing peak concurrency while the team is still validating the path end to end for the first time with real traffic. None of this guarantees a clean launch. It's what makes a clean launch the expected outcome rather than a lucky one -- and it's worth noting explicitly that a calm go-live under normal traffic patterns validates the migration itself, not every future condition the new platform will eventually face.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Final go/no-go checklist

Marcus walks the team through the checklist in the go-live meeting, with Celeste Marchbanks chairing the go/no-go decision:

```
GO-LIVE CHECKLIST -- Haverbrook Tickets cutover
  [x] Terraform apply (prod) -- clean, no drift (terraform plan: no changes)
  [x] EKS prod node groups -- healthy, capacity confirmed for 100% load
  [x] GitHub Actions pipeline -- green on main, last deploy < 24h ago
  [x] Prometheus / Grafana / Alertmanager -- dashboards live, alert routes tested
  [x] On-call rotation -- staffed for the cutover window + 48h after
  [x] Rollback plan -- documented, dry-run tested in staging
  [x] Support readiness -- Oscar Bennett's team briefed
  DECISION (Celeste Marchbanks): GO
```

## Step 2 -- Brief Support before anything moves

Oscar's team gets a short one-pager before the cutover window opens: what's changing (checkout now runs on the new AWS/EKS platform), what customers might notice (nothing, ideally), and who to escalate to -- Marcus, directly -- if anything looks unusual. Oscar also gets the same Grafana dashboard link the on-call engineer is watching, so his team can glance at real-time health themselves instead of guessing during a live customer call.

```
SUPPORT BRIEFING -- one-pager, distributed to Oscar Bennett's team
  What's changing: checkout and browse now run on AWS/EKS, not the
    legacy on-prem stack. Customer-facing behavior is unchanged.
  What you might see: nothing unusual. If you do, it likely shows
    up as a slow page load or a payment error message.
  Escalation path: message Marcus Oyelaran directly in #devops-oncall,
    don't wait for a ticket queue during the cutover window.
  Dashboard: Grafana link included for support leads to self-check.
```

## Step 3 -- Pick the window and set up the rollback path

The team schedules the cutover for a Tuesday mid-morning window -- a real but low-traffic period, deliberately not during an active on-sale. Rollback is a weight change, not a redeploy:

```
ROLLBACK PLAN (pre-tested in staging)
  Mechanism: ALB target group weighted routing
  New platform weight: adjustable 0-100 in increments
  Rollback action: set new-platform weight to 0, legacy weight to 100
  Expected rollback time: < 90 seconds, no customer-visible restart
```

## Step 4 -- Stage 1: 10% of real traffic

```
CUTOVER STAGE 1 -- 10% real traffic to new platform
  Duration observed: 20 minutes

  Error rate: 0.08% (baseline: 0.11%)
  Pods: stable, no HPA scaling events, no restarts
  Decision: proceed to Stage 2
```

  Duration observed: 25 minutes

lessons.title: Checkout Is Failing and Nobody Got Paged
lessons.summary: A 90-minute outage at VoltPay, Haverbrook Tickets' payment processor, quietly breaks real checkouts while every dashboard says the system is healthy -- until Oscar Bennett's support queue forces Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy to go looking themselves, and find something no HTTP-status alert was ever built to see.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Weeks after a clean go-live, VoltPay -- the external payment processor checkout-api calls to actually charge a customer's card -- starts failing. Not down outright, but badly degraded: a real partial outage, roughly 90 minutes long, where a meaningful share of real checkout attempts time out waiting on a VoltPay response.

checkout-api already has code for this, written long before this project, and it's reasonable code: rather than returning a scary 5xx for a declined or timed-out payment, it returns a clean `200 OK` with `{"orderStatus": "failed", "reason": "payment_timeout"}`, so the frontend can show the customer a normal "your payment didn't go through" message instead of treating a card problem like a server crash. During this outage, that reasonable design becomes invisible camouflage: every HTTP-status-based metric, every Grafana panel, every alert built around "a 5xx response is an error" sees nothing but 200s and stays silent.

This lesson is the investigation. Oscar Bennett's support queue starts filling with real complaints about 30-40 minutes into the outage, and escalates to Celeste Marchbanks and Marcus. Marcus and Ananya's first move is the dashboards -- and the dashboards are green: normal HTTP error rate, healthy pods, no Kubernetes-level anomaly anywhere. Confused by a support queue full of angry customers and a monitoring stack insisting nothing is wrong, Marcus goes around the HTTP layer entirely and queries the orders database directly for `orderStatus = 'failed'` counts. The real number is dozens of times the normal baseline. Tracing a sample of those failed orders, he and Ananya find every one of them is the same thing: a VoltPay timeout, wrapped in a 200. The lesson ends at that moment -- the team now understands exactly what happened and why nothing caught it, but nothing has been fixed yet.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a smoke detector that's wired to a special sensor that only detects orange flames. One day a fire starts that burns a strange shade of blue -- plenty of smoke, plenty of heat, real danger -- but because it's the wrong color of flame, the detector never makes a sound. Everyone in the house has to actually smell the smoke themselves before anyone realizes anything's wrong.

That's what happens at Haverbrook Tickets. The system that pays for tickets has a payment partner, and that partner has a bad 90-minute stretch where it's too slow to actually charge anyone's card. The checkout system handles that politely -- it tells the customer "your payment didn't work, try again" instead of showing a scary error page. But the alarm the team built only listens for scary error pages. A polite "your payment didn't work" message doesn't trip it, no matter how many times it happens.

So for over half an hour, real people are failing to buy tickets, and every screen the team is watching says everything is fine -- until enough customers call in annoyed that someone finally goes and checks by hand, and finds a mess the alarm was never built to notice.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The diagnostic sequence here is the part worth studying as closely as the finding itself, because it's a textbook case of a monitoring stack reporting ground truth about the wrong layer. Marcus and Ananya's first instinct -- check the dashboards -- is the correct first instinct; it just happens to return a false negative, because HTTP status code, pod health, and CPU/memory are all genuinely, accurately normal. The infrastructure is healthy. The business outcome is not. Those are different claims, and nothing in the stack as built distinguishes them.

What breaks the stalemate is going around the instrumentation layer entirely and querying the orders database directly for the one signal that actually reflects customer experience: `orderStatus = 'failed'` counts over the incident window, compared against baseline. That number -- dozens of times normal -- is the first real evidence that something is wrong, and it arrives only because someone thought to ask a question the dashboards weren't built to answer.

Tracing a sample of those failed orders from there is what converts "something's wrong with order outcomes" into a precise mechanism: every sampled failure traces back to the same VoltPay timeout, wrapped in checkout-api's existing graceful `200 OK` handling. That handling was a deliberate, reasonable product decision, made independently and before this infrastructure project existed. The error-rate alert, built on "a 5xx response is an error," was never wired to the signal that would have caught this -- not because anyone built it carelessly, but because nobody connected the alert's own definition of "error" back to a failure-handling behavior that already existed in the service it was watching. Quantifying the damage is the last piece before anyone touches a fix: across the roughly 90-minute window, an estimated 2,200-2,600 real checkout attempts failed this way -- more than 40 times the normal baseline failure rate for that time of day -- and it took about 35 minutes of customers calling Support before anyone outside that queue even suspected a problem, with another 20-25 minutes of investigation after escalation before the mechanism was understood. The lesson ends there: diagnosed, scoped, not yet fixed.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- VoltPay degrades, and checkout-api does exactly what it was built to do

VoltPay starts timing out on a meaningful share of real payment authorization calls. checkout-api's existing, pre-dating-this-project code handles that gracefully -- by design, not by accident:

```json
// checkout-api response to a VoltPay timeout -- HTTP 200
{
  "orderStatus": "failed",
  "reason": "payment_timeout",
  "orderId": "ORD-88214"
}
```

A clean 200 so the frontend shows the customer a normal "your payment didn't go through" message, not a scary server-error page. Every HTTP-status-based signal in the stack sees a 200 and moves on.

## Step 2 -- Support starts getting real complaints

About 30-40 minutes into the outage, Oscar Bennett's queue starts filling up:

```
SUPPORT QUEUE -- unusual volume, checkout complaints
  "Card got charged but I never got my tickets"
  "Checkout just spins and then says try again"
  "Tried 3 times, same error every time"
  Volume: 40+ tickets in 35 minutes (baseline: 2-3/hour)
```

Oscar escalates to Celeste Marchbanks and Marcus Oyelaran directly.

## Step 3 -- Marcus and Ananya check the dashboards first -- and they're green

```
Grafana -- checkout-api, last 60 minutes
  HTTP error rate (5xx): 0.09%   (baseline 0.08%) -- NORMAL
  Pod health: 12/12 Running, 0 restarts -- NORMAL
  CPU / memory: nominal -- NORMAL
  Alertmanager: 0 active alerts (CheckoutApiHighErrorRate not firing)
```

Every infrastructure-level signal says the system is healthy. Nothing has fired.

## Step 4 -- Marcus goes around the HTTP layer and queries the orders database directly

Confused by the mismatch, Marcus queries real order outcomes instead of HTTP status:

```sql
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('minute', created_at) AS minute_bucket,
  COUNT(*) AS failed_orders
FROM orders
WHERE order_status = 'failed'
  AND created_at BETWEEN '2026-10-21 14:00' AND '2026-10-21 15:30'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
```

```
  14:05   3 failed    (baseline: ~1/5min)
  14:20  38 failed
  14:35  61 failed
  14:50  74 failed
  15:05  52 failed
  15:20  11 failed    (VoltPay recovering)

  Total this window: ~2,400 failed orders
  Normal baseline for this window: ~55 failed orders
  Roughly 40x normal.
```

## Step 5 -- Trace a sample and find the mechanism

Ananya and Marcus pull ten failed orders from the window and trace each one's checkout-api logs:

```
ORD-88214  reason: payment_timeout  VoltPay call: 30.1s, timed out
ORD-88229  reason: payment_timeout  VoltPay call: 29.8s, timed out
ORD-88241  reason: payment_timeout  VoltPay call: 30.0s, timed out
... (7 more, identical pattern)
Result: 10 of 10 are VoltPay timeouts, every one returned as HTTP 200.
```

## Step 6 -- Write up the diagnosis

```
DIAGNOSIS -- checkout failures invisible to monitoring
Root cause: VoltPay partial outage (~90 min) caused widespread
payment timeouts. checkout-api's existing graceful handling
returns HTTP 200 for a declined/timed-out payment by design.
The production alert (CheckoutApiHighErrorRate) defines "error" as
any 5xx response, so this failure class could never have triggered
it -- at any volume.
Scope: ~2,400 failed checkouts, ~40x baseline, over ~90 minutes.
Detection: Support queue, ~35 min after onset. No automated alert fired.
Status: Diagnosed. Not yet fixed.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Traced a ~90-minute VoltPay partial outage to ~2,400 failed checkouts (~40x baseline), all returned by checkout-api as HTTP 200 with orderStatus=failed per its existing graceful-handling design. The CheckoutApiHighErrorRate alert defines error as any 5xx response, so it was structurally incapable of catching this regardless of volume. Found via direct orders-table query after dashboards and Alertmanager showed nothing abnormal. Diagnosed, not yet fixed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We had a real checkout outage today caused by our payment processor, VoltPay, and our monitoring didn't catch it automatically -- Support's complaint volume is what surfaced it, about 35 minutes in. We now know exactly why it slipped through and roughly how many customers it affected, and we're moving straight into building the fix.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Earlier today, a problem with our payment processor caused a real but temporary disruption to checkout -- roughly 2,400 attempted purchases over about 90 minutes were affected before our team identified it. Our automated alerts didn't catch this particular type of failure, which we've now fully diagnosed, and we're implementing the fix today to make sure this specific gap can't happen again.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing the Alerting Gap
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy build a business-outcome metric and alert that doesn't depend on HTTP status, add a synthetic VoltPay canary check that runs independent of real traffic, flag checkout-api's failure-reason visibility gap to Lin Chao, and write a standing review step so the next alert gets built against how a service actually fails.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Diagnosing last lesson's incident only answers "why didn't we catch it." This lesson answers "what makes sure we catch the next one" -- and the fix has four distinct parts, because a single alert tweak would patch this one symptom without closing the underlying gap.

First, Marcus and Ananya add a new metric that checkout-api increments itself, based on the business outcome of an order rather than the HTTP status code it happens to return -- `checkout_orders_total{status="succeeded"}` and `checkout_orders_total{status="failed"}` -- and build a new Prometheus alert on the *failure rate* of that metric, which fires regardless of what HTTP status code accompanied the failure.

Second, because a failure-rate alert still depends on real customer traffic to generate signal, they add a synthetic canary: a small scheduled job that runs a real, sandboxed end-to-end checkout against VoltPay's test mode every few minutes, independent of whether any real customer happens to be checking out right now -- so a VoltPay-side problem gets caught even during a quiet 3 a.m. lull, not just during a busy afternoon.

Third, Marcus raises a concern with Lin Chao's team: infrastructure-level alerting shouldn't have to guess at business outcomes by inferring them from HTTP status. He asks them to consider exposing checkout-api's internal failure reason through a response header or a dedicated metrics endpoint, so this kind of tooling-to-application gap is less likely to recur as the service evolves.

Fourth, and least technical but arguably most durable, the team documents a standing review step in their alert-build process: any time a new alert is built against an existing service, check whether that service has any non-standard response behavior -- like a deliberate 200 on a handled failure -- that the alert's assumptions don't account for. The lesson closes on the broader lesson learned: a service can be technically healthy -- 200s, green pods, normal CPU -- while the thing customers actually care about is completely broken, and an alert is only as good as how closely its definition of "error" matches how the service actually fails.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the smoke detector that only noticed orange flames and missed the blue one? This lesson is the team going back and fixing that detector properly, in four ways.

First, they stop asking the smoke detector to guess what's happening from the color of the flame, and instead wire a sensor directly to the thing that actually matters: did the ticket purchase work or not, as a fact, no color-guessing involved.

Second, they add a second line of defense: a little robot that walks through buying a test ticket every few minutes, all day and all night, even when no real customers happen to be shopping right then -- so even a quiet 3 a.m. problem gets noticed right away instead of waiting for a real customer to stumble into it.

Third, they go talk to the people who built the checkout system in the first place and ask: could you leave us a clearer note next time about exactly why something failed, instead of making us guess?

Fourth, they write themselves a reminder for next time: whenever we build a new alarm, check first whether this particular room has anything unusual about it that might fool the alarm -- the way the blue flame fooled this one.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Each of the four fixes targets a different layer of the same failure, which is why a single alert tweak wouldn't have been sufficient. The new business-outcome metric moves the source of truth from an inferred signal (HTTP status, a proxy for success that happened to be wrong in this one case) to an authoritative one (the service's own declaration of what actually happened to the order) -- a materially different reliability guarantee, not just a different metric name.

The synthetic canary closes a separate, real gap that a passive metric alone can't: a failure-rate alert on real traffic only generates signal when there's traffic to measure, and a genuinely rare but severe problem during a low-volume window can hide in small numbers even with the correct metric in place. An active, scheduled, sandboxed checkout against VoltPay's own test mode generates signal on a fixed cadence regardless of real customer behavior, which is precisely the property a dependency-health check needs.

Flagging the header/metrics-endpoint gap to Lin Chao's team addresses something neither of the first two fixes can: the structural mismatch between what infrastructure tooling can observe (HTTP-level signals) and what the business actually needs to know (why an order failed). That's not a monitoring problem to solve with more Prometheus rules -- it's an API design question that belongs with the team that owns checkout-api's application logic, and routing it there instead of working around it is the more durable fix.

The standing review step is the only one of the four that isn't a piece of infrastructure -- it's a process control, and it's the one most likely to prevent the *next*, different version of this same class of mistake. The failure mode here wasn't "the alert was built badly"; it was "the alert's designers never checked the target service's existing behavior against the alert's own assumptions." A checklist item that forces that check doesn't require anyone to have already learned this lesson the hard way again.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Part 1 -- A business-outcome metric and a failure-rate alert that doesn't need HTTP status

Marcus and Ananya add a counter inside checkout-api itself, incremented based on the actual order outcome, not the HTTP response it happens to send:

```javascript
// checkout-api, order completion handler
const checkoutOrdersTotal = new prom.Counter({
  name: "checkout_orders_total",
  help: "Checkout attempts by business outcome, independent of HTTP status",
  labelNames: ["status", "reason"],
});

// on every order resolution, regardless of HTTP status returned:
checkoutOrdersTotal.inc({ status: "succeeded", reason: "none" });
// ...or, on a VoltPay timeout/decline:
checkoutOrdersTotal.inc({ status: "failed", reason: "payment_timeout" });
```

A new alert watches the failure *rate* of this metric, not any HTTP signal:

```promql
sum(rate(checkout_orders_total{status="failed"}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(checkout_orders_total[5m]))
> 0.05
```

```
ALERT: CheckoutBusinessFailureRateHigh
  Fires on: checkout_orders_total failure ratio > 5% over 5m
  Independent of: HTTP status code entirely
  Would have fired: ~9 minutes into the VoltPay outage, not 35
```

## Part 2 -- A synthetic canary that doesn't wait for real traffic

A scheduled job runs a real, sandboxed end-to-end checkout against VoltPay's test mode every few minutes, so a VoltPay problem is caught even during a quiet period:

```yaml
# k8s/checkout-canary-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: checkout-canary
spec:
  schedule: "*/3 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: checkout-canary
              image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/checkout-canary:latest
              env:
                - name: VOLTPAY_MODE
                  value: "sandbox"
                - name: TARGET
                  value: "https://checkout-api.internal/orders"
          restartPolicy: Never
```

The canary pushes a simple success/failure gauge, and a short alert fires on consecutive misses:

```promql
checkout_canary_success == 0
```

```
ALERT: CheckoutCanaryFailing
  Fires on: 2 consecutive failed canary runs (6 minutes)
  Catches: VoltPay-side problems with zero dependency on real traffic volume
```

## Part 3 -- Flag the visibility gap to Lin Chao's team

Marcus opens a ticket with Lin Chao's application team rather than working around the gap in infrastructure alone:

```
TICKET -- checkout-api: expose internal failure reason to infra tooling
Problem: Infra-level monitoring currently has to infer business
outcome from HTTP status, which checkout-api's own graceful-failure
design (200 on a handled payment failure) makes unreliable.
Ask: Consider exposing the internal failure reason via either
  (a) a response header, e.g. X-Checkout-Outcome: failed,
  (b) a dedicated /metrics endpoint infra tooling can scrape directly.
Owner: Lin Chao's team (checkout-api application logic)
Status: Raised, not yet scheduled -- for the team's roadmap.
```

## Part 4 -- A standing review step for every future alert

The team adds a permanent line item to their alert-build checklist:

```
ALERT-BUILD REVIEW CHECKLIST -- new permanent item
  [ ] Does the target service have any non-standard response
      behavior (e.g., 200 on a handled/expected failure) that
      this alert's assumptions don't account for?
  [ ] Confirmed by reading the service's own failure-handling
      code, not just its documented happy-path behavior.
```

## Closing the loop

```
LESSON LEARNED
A service can be technically healthy -- 200s, green pods, normal
CPU and memory -- while the thing customers actually care about
is completely broken. An alert is only as good as how closely its
definition of "error" matches how the service it watches actually
fails, not the generic default.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Shipped a business-outcome metric (checkout_orders_total by status/reason, incremented by checkout-api itself) with a new failure-rate alert independent of HTTP status, plus a 3-minute synthetic canary against VoltPay sandbox mode so a dependency failure is caught without needing real traffic. Opened a ticket with Lin Chao's team to expose checkout-api's internal failure reason via header or metrics endpoint, and added a permanent 'check for non-standard response behavior' step to our alert-build checklist.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've closed the gap that let the VoltPay incident go unnoticed by automated monitoring. The fix has four parts: a new way to measure real checkout failures directly, a background check that catches payment-processor problems even with no customers currently checking out, a request to the application team for clearer failure signaling, and a permanent step in our process so we check for this type of gap on every future alert we build.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've put a permanent fix in place for the checkout monitoring gap from earlier today. Going forward, we'll detect this type of payment-processor problem within minutes instead of relying on customer complaints, including during quiet overnight hours when very few customers are shopping. We've also updated our internal process so every future alert we build gets checked against this exact kind of blind spot before it ships.

lessons.title: Presenting the Real Incident and the Fix, Honestly
lessons.summary: Marcus Oyelaran presents the finished Haverbrook Tickets build and the VoltPay checkout incident to Celeste Marchbanks and engineering leadership -- real framing of what shipped on AWS/EKS, and full honesty about the alerting gap's discovery and fix.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the whole engagement reports back. Over sixteen prior videos, Marcus Oyelaran and the Haverbrook Tickets platform team took catalog-api and checkout-api from a manual, unmonitored state to a real AWS deployment: Terraform-managed infrastructure, container images built in CI and pushed to Amazon ECR, a staged rollout across dev, staging, and prod EKS clusters through GitHub Actions, and Prometheus, Grafana, and Alertmanager watching production. That build went live successfully -- and then, during a genuine VoltPay partial outage, it also surfaced a real blind spot: checkout-api's error-rate alert, defined purely as 'non-2xx HTTP status,' could not see a payment failure that the application deliberately returned as HTTP 200. For roughly 90 minutes, checkouts were silently failing while every dashboard showed green.

In this video, Marcus stands in front of Celeste Marchbanks, Haverbrook's VP of Engineering and the project's business sponsor, and presents both halves honestly: the real infrastructure and monitoring that is now live and doing its job, and the specific gap that let a real incident run for 90 minutes before anyone outside Customer Support noticed. The goal of this presentation is not to minimize the incident or to bury it under a wall of infrastructure slides -- it's to show Celeste that the team's own monitoring investigation found it, explained it precisely, and fixed it in a way that makes the same failure mode visible next time.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a security guard at a building whose only job is to notice anyone who breaks a window to get in. One day, someone picks the lock on a side door instead -- no broken glass, nothing for the guard to see -- and walks right past, carrying things out for an hour and a half before a customer at the front desk finally says, 'hey, didn't that person just walk out with your inventory?' The guard's rule wasn't wrong, exactly -- it just never covered this way of getting in.

That's what happened at Haverbrook Tickets. The alert that was supposed to catch checkout problems only watched for one kind of 'broken window' -- a server error code. When the payment company VoltPay had a partial outage, checkout-api handled it the way it was built to: it told the customer 'this didn't work' in a normal, polite way, which looked exactly like a normal response to the alert. Customers trying to buy tickets kept hitting that silent failure for about 90 minutes before Haverbrook's own support team started getting complaints and said something. Marcus and Ananya Reddy went and found the real count of failures by looking directly at the orders themselves, found the real number was way higher than normal, and traced it back to the alert's blind spot. Now Marcus has to stand up and tell his boss, Celeste, exactly what happened and exactly what they did about it -- not just that everything's fine now.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A leadership readout about a production incident succeeds or fails on one decision: whether the presenter treats the fixed blind spot as proof the monitoring investment works, or tries to talk around it. This lesson is built around the former. The headline deserves to be stated first, plainly, because it's real: catalog-api and checkout-api are running on Amazon EKS across dev, staging, and prod, built and deployed through a GitHub Actions pipeline that pushes images to ECR, provisioned by Terraform, observed by Prometheus/Grafana/Alertmanager, and already carrying real production traffic for Haverbrook Tickets' roughly 500,000 monthly active users.

Naming the incident by its exact mechanism -- not 'there was a monitoring issue' but 'checkout-api returns HTTP 200 with orderStatus: "failed" on a VoltPay timeout or decline, which is a reasonable application design choice, and the production alert defined "error" purely as a non-2xx HTTP status, so it structurally could not detect this failure mode no matter how severe it got' -- is what lets Celeste trust the fix rather than just accept an apology. It is also important to state plainly that checkout-api's behavior was never the bug; returning a clean 200 with a structured failure status is a defensible API design. The defect lived entirely in the alert's definition of 'error,' which assumed one specific failure shape without checking whether that assumption held for every service it watched.

The reframe that keeps this presentation honest rather than defensive is that Oscar Bennett's Customer Support team noticing a wave of complaints roughly 30 to 40 minutes into a 90-minute incident -- followed by Marcus and Ananya tracing the real failure count directly from the orders database rather than from any dashboard -- is the team's own diagnostic process working, even though it worked later than anyone would have wanted. No payment was charged incorrectly and no order data was lost; the orders table had the true picture the entire time, it just wasn't being watched the right way. That distinction -- a monitoring gap, not a data-integrity failure -- is the one Celeste most needs to hear stated precisely.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with what this presentation actually covers, before the incident

Tell the room directly: this update covers two things, in order. First, the real infrastructure and monitoring build that is now live in production for catalog-api and checkout-api. Second, a real incident that build's own monitoring caught -- how it happened, how it was found, and how it's fixed. Lead with the first part. A presentation that buries a genuinely successful build under nothing but incident detail reads as more alarming than the situation actually is.

## Step 2 -- State what's live, plainly, first

```
HAVERBROOK TICKETS -- WHAT'S ACTUALLY RUNNING TODAY

Services:     catalog-api (Node.js), checkout-api (Python/FastAPI,
              integrates with VoltPay)
Infra:        AWS, provisioned by Terraform; images built and pushed
              to Amazon ECR
Clusters:     Amazon EKS -- dev, staging, prod, with a staged rollout
              between them
CI/CD:        GitHub Actions, build -> test -> deploy
Monitoring:   Prometheus + Grafana dashboards + Alertmanager paging
Status:       Live, serving real traffic for ~500K monthly active
              users, load-tested before go-live
```

Lead with this block before saying one word about VoltPay.

## Step 3 -- Name the incident by its exact mechanism

```
MARCUS: During a VoltPay partial outage, checkout-api did exactly
        what it was built to do -- when a payment times out or gets
        declined, it returns a normal HTTP 200 with orderStatus set
        to "failed," instead of a server error. That's a reasonable
        design choice on Lin Chao's side; it lets the frontend show a
        clean, specific failure message instead of a generic error
        page. The problem was ours: the production error-rate alert
        Ananya and I built defined "error" purely as a non-2xx
        status code, so it had no way to ever see this failure mode,
        no matter how many checkouts failed this way.
```

## Step 4 -- Explain who caught it, and how, without softening the timeline

Say this plainly: "The incident ran about 90 minutes. Every one of our dashboards showed green the entire time. Oscar Bennett's Customer Support team was the first to notice, around 30 to 40 minutes in, from a real wave of customer complaints -- not from anything we built. Once Ananya and I were looped in, we didn't trust the dashboards; we queried the orders database directly for orderStatus = 'failed' counts, found the real failure rate was running dozens of times above normal, and traced it back to the alert's blind spot from there."

## Step 5 -- State the fix, specifically

```
FIX, FOUR PARTS:
1. New business-outcome metric counting checkout successes and
   failures by orderStatus, independent of HTTP status code.
2. New alert on that metric's failure rate -- catches this exact
   failure mode, and others like it, going forward.
3. A synthetic/canary checkout running end-to-end every few minutes,
   independent of real customer traffic.
4. A request to Lin Chao's team to expose checkout failure reasons
   more clearly from checkout-api itself.
```

## Step 6 -- Frame the good news correctly

The right frame is not "we missed something and got lucky Oscar's team noticed." It's: "our own investigation -- once alerted by Support -- found the real failure count directly from the data we actually trust, identified the precise reason our own alert couldn't see it, and fixed the alert's definition, not just this one incident." No checkout data was lost and no customer was double-charged; the orders table told the truth the entire time, it just wasn't being watched correctly.

## Step 7 -- Rehearse the hard questions

```
Q: Why did it take 30-40 minutes for anyone internal to notice?
A: Because our only automated signal was the error-rate alert, and it
   structurally couldn't fire for this failure mode. Support noticing
   from real complaints was the actual first signal we had.

Q: Could the same blind spot exist in another alert right now?
A: Possibly -- we fixed this specific alert, but we have not yet gone
   back through every other alert in the system checking for the same
   class of gap. That's real, named follow-up work, not something
   we're claiming is done.
```

## Step 8 -- Close by asking for explicit understanding, not applause

Ask Celeste and the rest of leadership to confirm they understand two things clearly: why a non-2xx-only alert was never going to catch this, and that the new business-outcome alert and synthetic canary are both live in production today. That confirmation, not a smooth delivery, is what this presentation is actually for.

lessons.title: From Alerts to Action: How On-Call Works Now
lessons.summary: Translating the fixed monitoring into Marcus Oyelaran's and Ananya Reddy's actual on-call day -- what a real page looks like now, how the synthetic canary fits into daily operations, and the honest boundary: a single AWS region with no disaster recovery, and other existing alerts not yet re-audited for the same blind spot.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the incident presented and the fix live, this video follows the new monitoring the rest of the way -- out of the postmortem and into an actual on-call week for Marcus Oyelaran and Ananya Reddy. A checkout failure rate climbs; the new business-outcome alert fires through Alertmanager; whoever is on call gets paged with a specific signal -- 'checkout failure rate by orderStatus is above threshold' -- not a vague 'something's wrong.' This video walks that page from trigger to resolution, and shows how the synthetic canary check -- running an end-to-end checkout every few minutes, independent of real customer traffic -- fits into the same daily rhythm, catching a problem even on an hour when real traffic happens to be light.

It also states, honestly and without apology, two real boundaries that remain. First, Haverbrook Tickets runs entirely in a single AWS region today; there is no multi-region failover or disaster-recovery setup, so a region-level AWS outage would take the whole platform down, not just checkout. That idea was named and deferred back in lesson 3 as a real V2 direction, and it's restated here as still true, not hidden. Second, the team fixed checkout-api's specific alert, but nobody has gone back through every other alert in the system asking whether its definition of 'error' actually matches how that particular service can fail silently. That audit is real, valuable, and not yet done.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a fire alarm that used to only go off if it smelled smoke, but someone just installed a second alarm that also notices if the room gets dangerously hot even without visible smoke. Now when either alarm goes off, the people on duty know roughly what kind of problem to look for, and they also walk through the building every few minutes with their own flashlight, checking a few things by hand, just in case both alarms somehow miss something. That's a much better setup than before.

But it's still true that this building only has one fire escape route out of one side of the building -- if that whole side ever became unusable, everyone would still be stuck, and nobody has gone around yet checking whether any of the OTHER alarms in the building have the same old smoke-only blind spot the first one did. Marcus and Ananya are honest about both of those things. The new alarm for checkout is real and better. The building's other real limits are also real, and they say so out loud instead of pretending the building is now perfectly safe.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Monitoring only earns its investment the moment it maps onto a real on-call shift -- an alert that's technically well-designed but that nobody can describe in terms of 'what I actually do at 2 a.m. when this pages me' has failed at adoption even if it never failed a design review. The new business-outcome alert maps onto four concrete moments: trigger (checkout failure rate by orderStatus crosses a defined threshold, calculated independently of HTTP status code), page (Alertmanager routes it to whichever of Marcus or Ananya is on call, with the specific metric and threshold in the page itself), triage (the on-call engineer checks the business-outcome dashboard first, not the old HTTP-status dashboard, to see whether the spike is VoltPay-side, checkout-api-side, or something else), and escalation (if the failure traces into checkout-api's own logic rather than an external dependency, it routes to Lin Chao's team, who own that service's application code).

The synthetic canary check runs on its own schedule, independent of real traffic, which matters specifically because the VoltPay incident happened during a period when real traffic volume alone wasn't enough to make the failure obvious fast. A canary that runs every few minutes regardless of real customer behavior would have caught this incident directly, and that's the honest, bounded claim worth making about it -- it is not a claim that it catches every possible future failure mode.

The honest boundary matters as much as the workflow. Haverbrook Tickets runs in a single AWS region; there's no cross-region failover, and a region-level outage takes the whole platform down, not just checkout. That was named back in lesson 3 as a real V2 idea, not an oversight being surfaced now. The second, more pointed gap: fixing checkout-api's alert closed one specific blind spot, but the team has not yet systematically walked every other alert in the system asking whether its definition of 'error' actually matches that specific service's own ways of failing silently. That audit is real, valuable follow-up work, explicitly not yet done.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Walk a real page from trigger to resolution

```
TRIGGER:     The business-outcome metric -- checkout failures by
             orderStatus, independent of HTTP status -- crosses its
             defined threshold.
PAGE:        Alertmanager routes the page to whichever of Marcus or
             Ananya is on call, naming the specific metric and
             threshold, not a generic "error rate high" message.
TRIAGE:      The on-call engineer opens the business-outcome Grafana
             dashboard first -- failures broken out by orderStatus --
             to see whether the pattern looks like a VoltPay-side
             issue, a checkout-api-side issue, or something new.
ESCALATION:  If the pattern traces into checkout-api's own logic
             rather than an external dependency like VoltPay, it
             routes to Lin Chao's team, who own that service's
             application code.
```

## Step 2 -- Show how the canary check fits into the same day

```
The synthetic/canary checkout runs an end-to-end checkout flow every
few minutes, on its own schedule, completely independent of real
customer traffic. This matters specifically because the VoltPay
incident happened in a window where real traffic volume alone didn't
make the problem obvious fast -- a scheduled canary check doesn't wait
for enough real customers to hit the same failure before it notices.
```

## Step 3 -- Give on-call a decision rule for a real page

```
IF the canary check itself fails:
    -> treat as a confirmed, real checkout problem immediately --
       it's not noisy customer-traffic variance, it's a controlled
       test failing
IF the business-outcome alert fires but the canary is still passing:
    -> check whether the failure is isolated to one VoltPay payment
       method or region before assuming a full outage
IF the failure traces into checkout-api's own code:
    -> escalate to Lin Chao's team rather than treating it as a
       monitoring or infrastructure issue
```

## Step 4 -- Name what this setup does NOT do, honestly

Haverbrook Tickets runs entirely in one AWS region today. There is no multi-region failover and no disaster-recovery setup -- a region-level AWS outage would take catalog-api, checkout-api, and the EKS clusters running them down together, not just checkout. This was named and deliberately deferred back in lesson 3 as a real V2 direction, not something discovered now.

## Step 5 -- Name the second gap just as plainly

```
NOT YET DONE: fixing checkout-api's alert closed one specific blind
spot -- an alert that defined "error" as non-2xx status, watching a
service that could fail silently with a 200. Nobody has yet gone back
through every OTHER alert in the system asking the same question:
does this alert's definition of "error" actually match how THIS
specific service can fail? That's real, valuable, not-yet-done work.
```

## Step 6 -- Name the real V2 idea honestly, as not yet built

```
NOT YET BUILT -- A CONCRETE V2 IDEA:
Multi-region deployment with real failover, so a single AWS region
outage doesn't take the whole platform down. Real, worth building,
named since early planning, not built yet.
```

## Step 7 -- Close the loop on what changed for on-call specifically

The real change isn't just "we added an alert." It's that a page now names a business outcome Marcus and Ananya can act on directly, a canary check runs on its own schedule instead of waiting on real traffic, and the team knows exactly which two things -- single-region risk and the un-audited alert fleet -- still need real, scoped work next.
